# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI

<note>original: "ḪAMMURABI"</note>

<note>The Code of Hammurabi is one of the most famous and well-preserved legal documents from the ancient world. Established by the Babylonian King Hammurabi (who reigned approximately 1792–1750 BCE), the code consists of nearly 300 laws and judgments. These laws were famously carved onto a seven-foot-tall black diorite stone (stele) and placed in a public square for all to see. The text covers a wide range of topics, including trade, labor, property, and family law.</note>

<note>The primary subjects for this page include: The Code of Hammurabi, Babylonian law, and the variant spelling <term>Hammurapi: A common alternative transliteration of the king's name from the original cuneiform script.</term></note>

<summary>This title page identifies the volume as "The Code of Hammurabi," establishing the focus on one of history's earliest and most significant legal systems. It introduces the reader to the foundational laws of the First Babylonian Dynasty.</summary>
<keywords>Code of Hammurabi, Babylonian law, Hammurapi, Mesopotamia, legal history, title page</keywords>

# ON CHAPTER 15.

## THE FIRST DOUBT.

<margin>In what the harmony between the Law and the Gospel consists.</margin>

Whether from the words of the Apostle: *you are not under the law, but under grace* <note>original: "non sub lege estis, sed sub gratia" — Romans 6:14</note>, it can be rightly inferred that the Law has been abolished by Christ?

I respond with Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> in the *Summa Theologica* [part 1-2, question 104, article 3 and following], that the **moral law**, insofar as it is the **law of nature**, has in no way been abolished, but rather confirmed and fulfilled by Christ. Truly, insofar as it was the **Mosaic law** <note>The specific legal and religious code given to the Israelites</note> binding only the Jewish people, it is said to be abolished, because the **grace** of Christ does not bind us to the ceremonies and judicial rules of the old law, but to that observance which is through charity and faith. For as Saint Augustine says in his book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 14: "The commandments of the law are the letter that kills, if the life-giving spirit of grace is missing."

---

## THE SECOND DOUBT.

<margin>Christ came not to destroy the Law but to fulfill it.</margin>

Whether Christ took away the burden and difficulty from the Law?

I respond that Christ did not take away the difficulty that comes from the commandments themselves; for the commandments of Christ are weightier and more perfect than the commandments of the Law, as is clear in Matthew 5 where Christ explains the Law. Rather, he took away the difficulty on our part by granting grace and the strength to fulfill them, which the Law by itself did not provide. Hence it is said: *My yoke is easy, and my burden is light.* <note>Matthew 11:30</note>

---

## THE THIRD DOUBT.

<margin>How the Law is said to kill.</margin>

How is that saying to be understood: *The letter kills, but the spirit gives life*? <note>2 Corinthians 3:6</note>

I respond with Saint Thomas in the same place [cited above], that the letter of the Law does not kill by itself, but "by accident" <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "accidental" cause is an indirect one; the Law itself is good, but it results in "death" because humans cannot follow it without divine help</note>; because by showing what sin is without granting grace, the Law gave an opportunity for sinning and for transgression. The Spirit, however, gives life, because it gives grace, through which the commandments of the Law can be fulfilled for eternal life. For the Law was like a tutor <note>original Latin: "pedagogus," from the Greek word for a guardian who guided children to school</note> leading us toward Christ.

# PREFACE.

---

In January, 1903, I planned to give a transliteration <note>The process of representing the sounds of cuneiform characters using the Latin alphabet.</note> and a translation of the <term>Code of Hammurabi<note>One of the oldest and most complete written legal codes, proclaimed by the Babylonian king Hammurabi, who reigned from 1792 to 1750 BCE.</note></term> in the July or October number of *The American Journal of Semitic Languages and Literatures*. It soon became evident that it would be necessary to make a careful study of the Text of the Code as published in photographic reproduction by <note>original: "Pater"</note> Father Scheil <note>Jean-Vincent Scheil (1858–1940) was the French Dominican scholar and Egyptologist who discovered the stele of Hammurabi in Susa.</note> in his excellent commentary on the Code. This study led to the <term>autographing<note>In scholarly work, this refers to the painstaking hand-drawing of original inscriptions (like cuneiform) to ensure every stroke is accurately represented for publication.</note></term> of the Text so as to make it available to students. Later, in consultation with my brother, President William Rainey Harper <note>The founding president of the University of Chicago and a distinguished scholar himself.</note>, it was decided to make the plan more complete and to publish the results of our studies in two volumes, the first to contain the Autographed Text, Transliteration, Translation, Index of Subjects, Lists of Proper Names, Signs, Numerals, Mistakes and Erasures; the second to discuss the Code in its connection with the <term>Mosaic Code<note>The laws found in the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, attributed to Moses; scholars of this era were deeply interested in comparing Babylonian law with Biblical law.</note></term>.

A Transliteration and Translation were made before August first, 1903. The Autographed Text was published in the October number (1903) of *The American Journal of Semitic Languages and Literatures*. The Lists of Signs, Numerals, Mistakes and Erasures were made ready in October and the first week of November and were printed in the January number (1904) of *The American Journal of Semitic Languages and Literatures*. Since August few changes have been made in the Translation. The Transliteration, however, has undergone many minor changes. Both were in final proofs when I received Müller's *The Laws of Hammurabi* <note>original: "Die Gesetze Hammurabis"</note> on December twenty-ninth, 1903, and Kohler and Peiser's *Hammurabi's Law* <note>original: "Hammurabi's Gesetz"</note> on January twelfth, 1904. I have accepted one reading from Müller in § 47, and I have added from Kohler-Peiser in a foot-note their transliteration of the difficult passage in the Epilogue, **41**, 103-104. I have made good use of the excellent translations of Winckler, and of my friend, Rev. C. H. W. Johns, of Queens College, Cambridge. The latter also sent me some of his unpublished notes, which have been helpful in places. The

# INTRODUCTION.

The Monument on which the Code of Hammurabi is engraved was found in December, 1901, and January, 1902, on the acropolis of Susa <note>An ancient city in modern-day Iran; it was the capital of the Elamite Empire where the stone was taken as war booty.</note> by an Expedition sent out by the French Government under the Director General, M. de Morgan <note>Jacques de Morgan, a French mining engineer and archaeologist.</note>. It is a block of black diorite <note>An extremely hard and durable volcanic rock, making it an ideal material for a lasting legal monument.</note>, nearly eight feet high, broken into three pieces which were easily re-joined. Another fragment was found which does not belong to this Monument, but which contains a text corresponding to Column 41, lines 72–80; this leads to the conclusion that another copy of this famous Code existed in Susa. 

On the front side <note>Original: "Obverse."</note> we have a sculpted relief showing King Hammurabi receiving the laws from the Sun God <note>The Babylonian god Shamash, the patron of justice and light.</note>, to which the story of Moses receiving the Ten Commandments <note>Original: "Ten Words," a literal translation of the Hebrew phrase *Aseret ha-Dibrot*.</note> from God corresponds. Under this relief are engraved sixteen columns of text, four and one-half of which form the <term>Prologue<note>An introductory section praising the King’s piety and his care for his subjects.</note></term>. There were originally five more columns on the front, but these have been cut off by the Elamite conqueror <note>Shutruk-Nahhunte, who likely erased the text to make room for his own inscription, though he never added one.</note>. On the back <note>Original: "Reverse."</note>, there are twenty-eight columns, the last five of which form the <term>Epilogue<note>A concluding section that invokes blessings on those who uphold the law and curses on those who deface it.</note></term>. There are many reasons for believing that this Code of Laws was published in many places. We may accept the opinion of Scheil and Winckler <note>Jean-Vincent Scheil and Hugo Winckler, pioneering scholars in the study of cuneiform and ancient Near Eastern history.</note> that the copy found at Susa may have been taken as plunder by Shutruk-Nahhunte (about 1100 B.C.) and brought to his Elamite capital. We have fragments of later copies on clay tablets and these have enabled me to restore the text in one or two places. These later fragments, with a letter-by-letter transcription and translation, will form one of the Appendices to Part II.

Hammurabi, identified by most scholars of the time with the Amraphel mentioned in the Bible <note>Genesis 14:1. While modern scholars often dispute this specific identification, Hammurabi remains one of the most significant figures of antiquity.</note>, was the sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon and reigned for fifty-five years, about 2250 B.C. <note>Modern historical dating now places Hammurabi’s reign later, approximately 1792–1750 B.C.</note> We have a good account of his life and deeds in the Letters which he wrote to Sin-idinnam <note>A high-ranking official or governor under Hammurabi.</note> and in *The Chronicle of the Kings of Babylon*, both of which have been edited with great care by Mr. L. W. King. From the Prologue and Epilogue we learn that he

It also introduces King Hammurabi as a historical and biblical figure, noting the sources used to reconstruct his life.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION

[Hammurabi] was a great soldier and a pious, god-fearing king, who destroyed all his enemies to the North and South, and made his people to dwell in peace and security. He codified the existing laws that the strong might not oppress the weak, that they should give justice to the orphan and widow, and for the righting of wrong. He rebuilt cities and canals, he restored temples and endowed them with means for sacrifices, he re-established cults, he reunited his people.

Society in the time of <term>Hammurabi<note>The sixth king of the First Babylonian Dynasty, reigning c. 1792–1750 BCE.</note></term> consisted legally of the following classes: 1) the <term>awîlum<note>A term for the highest social rank, including land-owners and elites.</note></term>, 2) the <term>muškênum<note>A commoner or "freeman" who held a social status between the elite and the enslaved.</note></term>, and 3) the <term>wardum-amtum<note>The class of male (wardum) and female (amtum) slaves.</note></term>, and their rights and privileges were clearly defined. The first, *awîlum*, included the house-holders, property owners, the wealthy and upper classes. *Awîlum* has been translated by *man* or *person*. In a few places, it is almost necessary to translate *gentleman* as over against *freeman*. The second, *muškênum*, has been variously translated, *pauper*, *poor man*, *serf*, *retainer*, etc. The etymology of the word goes to show that the *muškênum* was poor. He could, however, hold property and slaves. He was free. He held a position half-way between the *awîlum*, upper class man, and the *wardum-amtum*, slave. I have used the term *freeman*. The third class, *wardum-amtum*, consisted of male and female slaves. There was also a class of public servants which received subsidies from the government. It is difficult to determine the exact duties of these officers. I have translated *officer* (recruiting officer), *constable* (military messenger, police officer), and *taxgatherer* (one in the public service). (Compare the Index of Subjects.) The position of women, which was a high one legally, of concubines, devotees, etc., will be discussed in Part II.

The Text as presented in Plates I-LXXXII has been reconstructed and edited from the photographs published by Scheil in Volume IV, *Elamite-Semitic Texts* <note>original: "Textes Élamites-Sémitiques"</note> of the *Memoirs of the Delegation to Persia* <note>original: "Mémoires de la Délégation en Perse"</note> (Paris, Leroux, 1902). It was printed in the October (1903) number of THE AMERICAN JOURNAL OF SEMITIC LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES. Since then Ungnad's excellent article, “On the Syntax of the Laws of Hammurabi,” <note>original: "Zur Syntax der Gesetze Hammurabis"</note> has appeared in the *Journal of Assyriology* <note>original: "Zeitschrift für Assyriologie"</note>, November, 1903 (Vol. XVII, 4), and I have accepted and incorporated into my text the following

# INTRODUCTION

In the transliteration and translation, I have also accepted Winckler's <note>Hugo Winckler (1863–1913) was a German archaeologist and philologist who worked extensively on the Code.</note> reading *light* <note>original: [*nu-r*]a-am</note>, **40**, 21, for *emerging* <note>original: [*u-s*]i-am</note> which stands in my text. To edit a text from a photograph is a very different task from editing an original copy. No one can appreciate this more keenly than I. In fact, I am of opinion that an edition of an Assyrian or Babylonian text which is to be final must go back to the originals. Hence there may be room for difference of opinion in regard to many small wedges which are not essential to any form of the Signs in which they are found. Some restorations have been attempted, and in these I have for the most part followed Scheil <note>Jean-Vincent Scheil (1858–1940) was the French scholar who first discovered and translated the Code of Hammurabi monument.</note>. I have, however, been obliged to differ from him in some places. Only such restorations were made as seemed to me to be fairly certain. Others, which were less certain, have been put in the Transliteration.

In the Transliteration I have used the <term>mimation<note>The addition of the letter 'm' to the end of nouns, a characteristic of the Old Babylonian dialect.</note></term> with the ideograms following the forms which have a syllabic spelling. In many places I have distinguished <term>ḳ<note>An "emphatic" k-sound produced deeper in the throat, distinct from the standard 'k' in Semitic languages.</note></term> from k where no such distinction is made in the Text. Again, in many places, I have preferred to retain the k, where <term>ḳ</term> might have been used with accuracy. My readings in all these places are indicated in the Glossary.

The Translation which is placed opposite the Transliteration is rather literal. In most cases, the Babylonian idiom has been retained in the English, *for example* <note>original: *e. g.*</note>: to take a wife, to set one's face, to cast one's eyes upon, etc. In other cases, I have not hesitated to change the form of expression for the sake of clearness. An effort was made to avoid technical and legal language.

The Index to Subjects was made very complete to enable the reader to consult the Code with the greatest ease. In fact, it may be used as a commentary to the Code.

The Glossary has been arranged alphabetically. Under A, are placed all words beginning with *a*, *e*, *i*, *o*, *u*, and *w*. With the

With the exception of a few words—for example, **if** <note>original: *šumma*</note>, **no** <note>original: *la*</note>, **not** <note>original: *ul*</note>, **in** <note>original: *ina*</note>, **to** <note>original: *ana*</note>, **man/citizen** <note>original: *awîlum*</note>, etc.—it has been my aim to register every occurrence of every form found in the Code.

The List of Signs and Numerals was finished about November first, 1903, before the appearance of Arthur Ungnad's article, "On the Syntax of the Laws of Hammurabi" <note>original Latin/German title: *Zur Syntax der Gesetze Ḥammurabis*</note>, in the November (XVII. 4) number of the *Journal of Assyriology* <note>original abbreviation: *ZA*</note>. The values of No. 84, **ku**, **kum**, **kum** <note>The author is discussing how to phonetically read specific cuneiform wedges; see Jensen, *KB*, III, pp. 111, 113 and Hunger, *Divination by Cups among the Babylonians* (original: *Becherwahrsagung bei den Babyloniern*), p. 7</note>, No. 137, **sa**, **za**, No. 148, **ud**, **ut**, **tam**, No. 194, **ṣu**, **zum** <note>cf. Hunger, p. 7</note> had already been listed. I have, however, accepted two of Ungnad's suggestions: namely, the reading **slave/servant** <note>original: *wardu*</note>, instead of the older reading **servant** <note>original: *ardu*</note>, on account of the occurrence of the word for **slavery** <note>original: *wardûtu*</note>; and the substitution of **ar** for **ri** in column **11**, line 34, as noted in the List of Scribal Errors.

The values **mash** <note>original: *maš*</note> and **bar** <note>original: *bar*</note> are usually distinguished in the Code (see No. 34), and hence the reading **House of Ulmash** <note>original: *E.UL.MAŠ*</note> is to be preferred to **House of Ulbar** <note>original: *E.UL.BAR*</note>. For the reading **House of Mismis** <note>original: *E.MIŠ.MIŠ*</note> instead of **House of Dupdup** <note>original: *E.DUP.DUP*</note>, see Nos. 65 and 66. Note the two forms of **Temple/House** <note>original: *Ê*</note> listed in No. 121. The sign under No. 121, which has not been explained hitherto, has been identified as a <term>gunu</term> <note>A "gunu" is a cuneiform sign modified with additional parallel wedges to change its meaning or intensity.</note> of No. 148; see the List of Scribal Errors, column **36**, line 89. In No. 142, the symbols for **seed** <note>original: *ŠE.ZIR*</note> may be read as **seed** <note>original: *ziru*</note> and the symbols for **food/fodder** <note>original: *ŠÀ.GAL*</note> in No. 150 as **sustenance** <note>original: *ukullû*</note>. In No. 35, the symbol **NU.TUR**, as is well known, has the value of an **officer** <note>original: *labuttû*</note>; **NU.IŠ.SAR** has been read as **gardener** <note>original: *amēlu urḳu*</note> by Delitzsch, and **man of the orchard** <note>original: *zikaru-kirû*</note> by Langdon; **NU.TUK** has the value of a **destitute woman or orphan** <note>original: *ekûtu*</note>. These values will be noted in the Glossary. No. 80 has been read incorrectly until now. It occurs twice and has the value **flesh** <note>original: *šēru*</note> at **37**, 32 and **oracle** <note>original: *šīru*</note> at **43**, 27.

In List II, **180 QA** <note>A <term>QA</term> is a Babylonian unit of capacity, roughly equal to one liter.</note> seems too large a number for the last sign. This is the usual reading, but **90 QA** would suit the context better in the law in which it occurs. Compare sections §§ 271 and 272: If a man hire oxen, a wagon, and a driver, he shall pay **180 QA** of grain per day; if a man hire a wagon only, he shall pay **40 QA** of grain per day. In § 268, we have: If a man hire an ox to thresh, **20 QA** of grain is its hire.

# TRANSLITERATION AND TRANSLATION

<term>Transliteration</term> <note>the process of converting the characters of one alphabet or writing system into those of another</note> and <term>Translation</term> <note>the process of expressing the sense of words or text in another language</note>

xv

->INTRODUCTION<-

My methods may not be accepted by every scholar. I am aware that in column **38**, line 82, the phonetic spelling **gu-u** <note>original: "gu-u"; a way of writing a word by spelling out its sounds syllable-by-syllable</note> is usually preferred where the logogram **AMAT** <note>original Sumerian logogram; in this context, it refers to a specific cuneiform sign shape used for the sound "gu"</note> represents the sound **gu**. I have also decided to retain the sign **lu** in column **13**, line 62, which appears in the phrase **is not bright** <note>original Akkadian: *la illû*</note>. Furthermore, in column **32**, line 80, the sign that appears as **ba** is actually an unfinished **zu** <note>the ancient scribe likely failed to complete the final wedge-shaped marks of the character, making it look like a different letter</note>. 

In List IV, I have recorded only the most significant erasures <note>places where the ancient scribe scraped away a mistake on the wet clay or stone to rewrite it</note>. The list is organized as follows:
*   The first column shows what the scribe wrote originally.
*   The second column shows the sign as it was corrected.
*   The third column shows the sign that the scribe actually intended to write.

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI.

---

## THE LAWS

### § 1.—Column V, lines 26-32.

If a man <term>awīlum: specifically a free man or a member of the upper class</term> charges another man with a crime and accuses him of murder <note>original: "nērtam," implying a capital offense or slaying</note>, but cannot prove it, his accuser shall be put to death.

### § 2.—Column V, lines 33-56.

If a man charges a man with sorcery <note>original: "kišbī," referring to harmful magic or witchcraft</note> but cannot prove it, he who is charged with sorcery shall go to the **River God** <term>Nârim: the personified River, used here for the "Trial by Ordeal"</term>; he shall leap into the river. If the **River God** overcomes him, his accuser shall take possession of his house. If the **River God** purifies him and he remains unharmed, then he who charged him with sorcery shall be put to death, and he who leaped into the river shall take possession of the house of his accuser.

### § 3.—Column V, lines 57-67.

If a man comes forward in a case to bear false witness <term>ṣarrātim: lies or malicious testimony</term>, and does not prove the word that he has spoken, if that case is a capital case <note>original: "dīn napištim," a case involving a life</note>, that man shall be put to death.

### § 4.—Column V, line 68—Column VI, line 5.

If he comes forward to bear witness regarding grain or silver <note>original: "kaspim," the standard currency of the time</note>, <column-break/> he shall bear the penalty <note>original: "arān," the specific fine or punishment</note> of that case.

### § 5.—Column VI, lines 6-30.

If a judge <term>dayyānum</term> renders a judgment, gives a decision, or issues a sealed document <note>original: "kunukkam," a clay tablet impressed with a cylinder seal to make it official</note>, and later alters his judgment, they shall prove that that judge has changed the judgment he rendered, and he shall pay twelvefold the claim that was in that case. Furthermore, they shall expel him from his seat of judgment in the assembly, and he shall not return to sit with the judges in a case.

<summary>This page lists the opening statutes of the Code, focusing on legal integrity, the "River Ordeal" for sorcery, and strict penalties for false witnesses and corrupt judges. These laws establish that the burden of proof lies with the accuser and that judicial decisions must be final and honest.</summary>

<keywords>law, justice, false witness, murder, sorcery, River Ordeal, trial by water, judge, penalty, corruption</keywords>

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI.

---

## THE LAWS

### § 1. <gloss>False accusation</gloss>

¶ If a man <term>awīlum: a free man or a member of the upper class</term> brings an accusation against another man, charging him with a capital crime <note>original: "nērtam," implying murder or a crime punishable by death</note> but is unable to prove the charge, he, the accuser, shall be put to death.

### § 2. <gloss>Sorcery and the Trial by Water Ordeal.</gloss>

¶ If a man charges another with sorcery <note>original: "kišbī," referring to harmful or malevolent magic</note> and cannot prove it, the one who is charged with sorcery shall go to the **River** <term>Nârim: the personified River God, used as a divine judge in trials by ordeal</term>; he shall throw himself into the river. If the river overcomes him, his accuser shall take possession of his house and estate. If, however, the river proves that man to be innocent and he emerges unharmed, the one who accused him of sorcery shall be put to death. He who jumped into the river shall then take possession of the accuser's house.

### § 3. <gloss>Perjury in a capital case.</gloss>

¶ If a man comes forward in a case to bear false witness <note>original: "šībūt ṣarrātim," malicious or lying testimony</note>, or fails to prove the testimony he has given, if that case involves a person's life <note>original: "dīn napištim," a capital offense</note>, that man shall be put to death.

### § 4. <gloss>Perjury in other offenses.</gloss>

¶ If a man bears witness in a case involving bribes of grain or money <note>original: "kaspim," literally silver, the common currency</note>, <column-break/> he shall himself bear the penalty <note>original: "arān," the specific fine or punishment</note> that would have been imposed in that case.

### § 5. <gloss>Alteration of a final judgment.</gloss>

¶ If a judge <term>dayyānum: a judicial official appointed by the king</term> pronounces a judgment, renders a decision, and delivers a verdict that is duly signed and sealed, and afterward changes his judg- <note>The text cuts off mid-word at the end of the page; it refers to the severe penalties for a judge who reverses a completed legal ruling.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the opening five laws of Hammurabi's Code, which establish strict penalties for false accusations, perjury, and judicial misconduct. It notably describes the "River Ordeal," a ritualized test used to determine guilt or innocence in cases where human evidence was insufficient.</summary>

<keywords>Code of Hammurabi, Babylonian law, false accusation, sorcery, trial by ordeal, River God, perjury, capital punishment, judicial integrity, ancient justice</keywords>

...if he later changes his judgment, they shall convict that judge of changing the judgment he rendered, and he shall pay twelve-fold the claim <note>original: "rugummâm," the penalty or amount in dispute</note> that was in that judgment. Furthermore, in the assembly <note>original: "puḫrum," the public gathering of elders or citizens where legal matters were often finalized</note>, they shall remove him from his seat of judgment, and he shall not return, nor shall he sit with the judges in a legal case ever again.

### § 6. <gloss>Theft from Temple or Palace.</gloss>

¶ If a man <term>awīlum: a free citizen of the upper class</term> steals the property <term>ŠA.GA: possessions or goods</term> belonging to a god <note>referring to the temple treasury</note> or the palace, that man shall be put to death. Furthermore, the person who received the stolen property from his hand shall also be put to death.

### § 7. <gloss>Illegal purchase from a minor or slave.</gloss>

¶ If a man buys or receives for safekeeping <note>original: "maṣṣarūtim," a formal legal arrangement for guarding property</note> silver, gold, a male slave, a female slave, an ox, a sheep, a donkey, or anything else from the hand of a man's son <note>referring to a minor still under his father's legal authority</note> or a man's slave, without witnesses or a written contract <note>original: "riksātim," binding legal agreements</note>, that man is considered a thief; he shall be put to death.

### § 8. <gloss>Restitution for stolen animals and boats.</gloss>

¶ If a man steals an ox, a sheep, a donkey, a pig, or a boat—if it belongs to a god <note>the temple</note> or the palace, he shall pay thirty times its value. If it belongs to a commoner <term>MAŠ.EN.KAK: a member of the social class between the free elite and the slaves, often state-dependents</term>, he shall repay ten times its value. If the thief has nothing with which to make payment, he shall be put to death.

### § 9. <gloss>Procedure for recovering lost property.</gloss>

¶ If a man who has lost property <note>original: "mimmušu ḫalqu," his vanished things</note> finds his lost property in another man's possession, and the man in whose hand the property was found says, "A seller sold it to me; I bought it before witnesses," and the owner of the lost property says, "I will bring witnesses who know my lost property..."

## § 10.—VII, 48-61.

## § 11.—VII, 62-VIII, 3.

¶ If the owner of the lost property has not brought the witnesses who know his lost property, he is a liar <note>original: "ṣaar," meaning malicious, deceitful, or a fraud</note>; he has stirred up slander <note>original: "tuššam," referring to a false and malicious accusation</note>, and he shall be put to death.

## § 12.—VIII, 4-13.

¶ If the seller has gone to his fate <note>a common Mesopotamian euphemism for death</note>, the buyer shall take from the house <note>referring to the estate or assets</note> of the seller five-fold the claim of that case.

## § 13.—VIII, 14-24.

¶ If that man's witnesses are not nearby <note>not immediately available to testify</note>, the judges shall grant him a time-limit for up to six months; if within six months he has not brought his witnesses, that man is a liar; he shall bear the penalty of that case <note>meaning he must suffer the punishment that would have been inflicted on the accused had the charge been proven</note>.

### THE CODE OF HAMMURABI

### § 14.—VIII, 25–29.

25 If a man 26 the son of a man 27 who is a minor <note>original: "ṣihram," referring to a young child or a minor</note> 28 has stolen, 29 he shall be put to death.

### § 15.—VIII, 30–36.

30 If a man 31 either a male slave of the palace 32 or a female slave of the palace, 33 or a male slave of a commoner 34 or a female slave of a commoner <term>MAŠ.EN.KAK: a member of the "Mushkenu" class—free citizens who were often state dependents, ranked between the aristocracy and slaves</term>, 35 has led out through the city gate, 36 he shall be put to death.

### § 16.—VIII, 37–48.

37 If a man 38 either a male slave or a female slave 39 who is a fugitive 40 belonging to the palace 41 or to a commoner 42 in his house 43 has harbored, and 44 at the call 45 of the public crier <term>nagirim: an official herald who made public announcements, including the descriptions of runaway slaves</term> 46 has not brought them out, 47 the owner of that house 48 shall be put to death.

### § 17.—VIII, 49–58.

49 If a man 50 either a male slave or a female slave 51 who is a fugitive 52 in the open country 53 has captured and 54 to his owner 55 has driven <note>original: "irtediaššu," implying the act of leading or escorting the slave back</note> him, 56 two shekels of silver 57 the owner of the slave 58 shall give to him.

### § 18.—VIII, 59–67.

59 If that slave 60 his owner 61 will not name, 62 to the palace 63 he shall drive him; 64 his past <note>original: "warkazu," referring to his background or ownership history</note> 65 shall be investigated and 66 to his owner 67 they shall return him.

### § 19.—VIII, 68–IX, 4.

68 If that slave 69 himself 70 in his house 71 he has detained, 72 afterward the slave IX, 1 in his hand 2 is caught, 3 that man 4 shall be put to death.

### § 20.—IX, 5–13.

### § 14.

### § 15.

¶ If a man assists either a male or female slave of the palace, or a male or female slave of a commoner <term>MAŠ.EN.KAK: the "mushkenu" class, citizens who were legally free but often held a social rank between the aristocracy and slaves</term> to escape through the city gate, he shall be put to death.

### § 16.

¶ If a man harbors in his house a male or female slave who has fled from the palace or from a commoner, and does not bring that slave forth at the call of the public herald <term>nagirim: an official crier responsible for making public announcements, including descriptions of runaways</term>, the owner of that house shall be put to death.

### § 17.

¶ If a man captures a male or female slave, a fugitive, in the open country and brings that slave back to his owner, the owner of the slave shall pay him two shekels <term>shekel: a Babylonian unit of weight for silver, roughly 8.3 grams, used as a standard of value</term> of silver.

### § 18.

¶ If that slave will not name his owner, the captor shall bring him to the palace; they shall inquire into his history <note>original: "warkazu," referring to the slave's background or previous ownership</note> and they shall return him to his owner.

### § 19.

¶ If he detains that slave in his house and later the slave is found in his possession, that man shall be put to death.

### § 20.

¶ If the slave escapes from the hand of his captor, that man shall swear an oath <note>original: "it-ma," to swear by the name of a god or the king</note> to the owner of the slave and shall be released from liability.

### § 21.

¶ If a man breaks into a house <note>literally "makes a breach," referring to digging through the mud-brick walls of a home</note>, they shall put him to death in front of that breach and they shall bury him within it.

### § 22.—IX, 22-27.

If a man <term>awīlum: a free man of the upper class</term> commits a robbery <note>original: "ḫubbatum"</note> and is caught, that man shall be put to death.

### § 23.—IX, 28-45.

If the robber is not caught, the man who was robbed shall declare all that he has lost <note>original: "mimmašu halgam," his lost property</note> in the presence of God <note>likely referring to a local temple or an official oath-taking ceremony</note>; then the city <term>alum</term> and the governor <term>rabianu: a local mayor or official</term> in whose territory and district the robbery was committed shall replace for him whatever was lost.

### § 24.—IX, 46-50.

If a life is lost <note>original: "napištum," literally "breath" or "soul"</note>, the city and the governor shall pay one mina <term>mina: a unit of weight, approximately 500 grams, equivalent to 60 silver shekels</term> of silver to his kinsmen.

### § 25.—IX, 51-65.

If a fire breaks out in a man's house, and a man who has come to extinguish it casts his eye upon the household goods <note>original: "numat," property or furniture</note> of the householder and takes the household goods of the householder, that man shall be thrown into that fire.

### § 26.—IX, 66—X, 12.

### § 38. — XII, 22-30.

An officer <term>rēdûm: a soldier who received land in exchange for service</term>, a constable <term>bā'irum: literally "fisherman," a state worker or soldier</term>, or a rent-payer <term>nāši biltim: a tenant on royal land who pays a portion of his crop as tribute</term> may not deed <note>original: "i-ša-ad-da-ar", meaning to record in writing or assign</note> any of the field, garden, or house belonging to his state service <term>ilkum: the obligation of service tied to the land</term> to his wife or daughter, nor may he give it to settle a debt <note>This prevented the king's land from being transferred to people who could not perform the required military or labor service.</note>.

### § 39. — XII, 31-38.

From the field, garden, or house which he has purchased and thus acquired for himself, he may indeed deed portions to his wife or his daughter, and he may give such property to settle his debts <note>The law distinguishes between state-granted land, which must remain with the service-provider, and private property, which the individual is free to sell or gift.</note>.

### § 40. — XII, 39-48.

A woman, a merchant <term>tamkārum: a state-authorized trader or financier</term>, or another holder of state service <note>original: "il-kum a-hu-u-um", literally a "foreign" or "other" service holder</note> may sell their field, garden, or house. The buyer shall then perform the service <term>ilkum</term> associated with the field, garden, or house that he has purchased.

### § 41. — XII, 49-62.

If a man should barter <note>original: "u-bi-ih", referring to an exchange or trade</note> for the field, garden, or house of an officer, a constable, or a rent-payer, and provide balancing payments <term>niplātim: cash or goods given to make up the difference in value during a trade</term>, the officer, constable, or rent-payer shall return to his original field, garden, or house, and he shall also keep the balancing payments that were given to him <note>This law essentially voids any trade that would strip a soldier of his state land, penalizing the person who tried to acquire it.</note>.

### § 42. — XII, 63 — XIII, 5.

If a man rents a field for cultivation <note>original: "a-na ir-ri-šu-tim", a sharecropping or tenancy agreement</note> and does not produce grain in that field, they shall call him to account for not performing the necessary work in the field, and he shall give grain to the owner of the field based on the yields of his neighbors <note>Agricultural production was a matter of state security; if a farmer was lazy, he still owed the average harvest amount to the landlord.</note>.

### § 43. — XIII, 6-16.

If he does not cultivate the field at all but leaves it fallow <note>original: "it-ta-di", meaning to neglect or leave waste</note>, he shall give grain to the owner of the field based on the yields of his neighbors; furthermore, he shall plow <term>mâri: a deep plowing to break up uncultivated soil</term> and harrow the field he neglected, and only then return it to the owner of the field.

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI

### § 38. — XII, 22-30.

An officer <term>rēdûm: a soldier receiving land in exchange for service</term>, a constable <term>bā'irum: a state worker or fisherman-soldier</term>, or a rent-payer <term>nāši biltim: a tenant on royal land who pays a portion of his crop as tribute</term> may not deed <note>original: "i-ša-ad-da-ar", meaning to record in writing or assign</note> the field, garden, or house belonging to his state service <term>ilkum: the obligation of service tied to the land</term> to his wife or daughter, nor may he assign them to settle a debt.

### § 39. — XII, 31-38.

He may, however, deed to his wife or daughter a field, garden, or house which he has purchased and thus possesses as private property, or he may assign such property to settle a debt <note>The law distinguishes between land held as a "fief" from the king, which must remain with the service-provider, and private property, which the individual is free to sell or gift as they wish.</note>.

### § 40. — XII, 39-48.

A woman <note>Likely referring to a *nadītum*, a woman of high status often associated with a temple who could own property</note>, a merchant <term>tamkārum: a state-authorized trader or financier</term>, or another holder of state service <note>original: "il-kum a-hu-u-um", literally a "foreign" or "other" service holder</note> may sell their field, garden, or house. The purchaser shall then carry out the service obligations <term>ilkum</term> associated with the property he has purchased.

### § 41. — XII, 49-62.

If a man should barter <note>original: "u-bi-ih", referring to an exchange or trade</note> for the field, garden, or house of an officer, constable, or rent-payer and provides additional payments <note>OCR: "sureties"; likely referring to the "balancing payment" in an unequal trade</note>, the officer, constable, or rent-payer shall return to his field, garden, or house, and he shall keep the additional payments that were given to him <note>This law prevented people from tricking soldiers out of their state-assigned lands through lopsided trades; any such transaction was voided, and the officer kept the "boot" as a penalty against the buyer.</note>.

### § 42. — XII, 63-XIII, 5.

If a man rents a field for cultivation but does not produce any grain in that field, they shall call him to account because he has not performed the required work on the field. He shall give grain to the owner of the field based on the yields of the adjacent fields <note>Ancient Babylonian law focused on "expected yield." If a farmer was lazy, he still owed the landlord what the land *should* have produced.</note>.

### § 43. — XIII, 6-18.

If he does not cultivate the field at all and neglects it, he shall still give grain to the owner of the field based on the yields of the adjacent fields. Furthermore, the field which he neglected he must break up with hoes, harrow it, and then return it to the owner <note>This ensured the land was not returned to the owner as a weed-choked wasteland, which would require years of "breaking" to become productive again.</note>.

### § 44.—XIII, 17-34.

If a man leases a fallow <term>KI.KAL: uncultivated or "waste" land</term> field for three years for the purpose of reclamation <note>original: "te-ip-ti-tim", referring to the process of breaking and opening up new soil for cultivation</note>, but he becomes lazy and does not open up the field, then in the fourth year he must plow the field, harrow it <note>original: "i-mar-ra-ar u i-ša-ak-ka-ak", describing the technical process of preparing the soil</note>, and return it to the owner. Furthermore, he shall measure out ten <term>GUR: a large unit of dry capacity, roughly 300 liters</term> of grain for every ten <term>GAN: a unit of surface area, approximately 3.5 hectares</term> of land <note>The text uses "X" as a variable or standard measurement for the fine or yield expected from reclaimed land</note>.

### § 45.—XIII, 35-46.

If a man has leased his field to a tenant farmer for a fixed rent <term>biltum: an agreed-upon amount of the crop paid as rent</term> and has already received that rent, and afterward the god Adad <term>Adad: the Mesopotamian god of storms, rain, and lightning</term> floods the field or a disaster <note>original: "bi-ib-bu-lum", referring to a destructive flood or inundation</note> carries away the crop, the loss shall be the tenant's alone.

### § 46.—XIII, 47-57.

If he has not yet received the rent for his field, or if he has leased the field for a half-share or a third-share <note>original: "mi-iš-la-ni" (half) or "ša-lu-uš" (third)</note>, the tenant farmer and the owner of the field shall divide the grain that remains in the field according to the agreed-upon proportion <term>ap-ši-te-im: the ratio or share specified in the contract</term>.

### § 47.—XIII, 58-70.

If the tenant farmer, because he did not recover his expenses <note>original: "ma-na-ha-ti-šu", referring to the labor and costs invested in the previous year</note> in the previous year, expresses a desire to continue farming the field, the owner of the field shall not object. The tenant shall farm the field, and at the time of harvest, he shall take the grain according to the terms of his original contract.

### § 48.—XIII, 71-XIV, 17.

If a man has a debt <note>original: "hu-bu-ul-lum", an interest-bearing loan</note> and the god Adad floods his field, or a storm carries away the crop, or if the grain does not grow in the field due to a lack of water, in that year he does not need to return any grain to his creditor. He shall moisten his clay tablet <note>original: "dup-pa-šu u-ra-ad-da-ab", a symbolic and legal action where the debt contract was softened/wiped to indicate that interest for that year was cancelled</note> and he shall not pay any interest for that entire year.

### § 44.

¶ If a man leases an unreclaimed field <note>original: "uncultivated or waste land"</note> for three years to develop it, but neglects it and does not develop the field, then in the fourth year he must break up the soil with hoes, he shall hoe and harrow it, and he shall return it to the owner of the field. Additionally, he shall measure out ten <term>GUR: a Babylonian unit of capacity, approximately 300 liters</term> of grain for every ten <term>GAN: a unit of land area, roughly 3.5 hectares</term> of land.

### § 45.

¶ If a man leases his field to a tenant farmer for a fixed crop-rent <note>This refers to a set amount of grain agreed upon regardless of the harvest size.</note> and receives that rent, but later the god <term>Adad: the Mesopotamian deity of storms and weather</term> floods the field or a storm carries away the produce, the loss falls entirely upon the tenant farmer.

### § 46.

¶ If he has not yet received the rent for his field, and he has leased the field for either a one-half or a one-third share of the harvest, the tenant and the owner of the field shall divide the grain remaining in the field according to their agreed-upon proportions.

### § 47.

¶ If the tenant farmer hands over the cultivation of the field to another person—because in a previous year he was unable to earn a living from it <note>The text suggests a situation where a struggling farmer sub-leases to someone more capable.</note>—the owner of the field shall not object. Since the field has been cultivated, at the time of harvest the owner shall take his share of the grain according to the terms of his original contracts.

### § 48.

¶ If a man is in debt and <term>Adad</term> <note>The storm god is invoked here to represent natural disasters like floods.</note> floods his field and carries away the produce, or if the grain fails to grow due to a lack of water, he does not need to give any grain to his creditor for that year. He shall alter his <term>contract-tablet: a clay document recording the legal terms of a loan</term> <note>original: "he shall wet his tablet," a phrase meaning to soften the clay to change the terms or cancel interest</note> and he shall not pay any interest for that entire year.

### § 49.—XIV, 18-44.

¶ If a man takes money <note>original: "silver" (*kaspam*)</note> from a <term>merchant: a *tamkarum* acted as both a trader and a state-authorized money-lender</term>, and gives to the merchant a field prepared for planting with grain or sesame, saying to him: "Cultivate the field, and harvest and take whatever grain or sesame is produced," if a tenant farmer <note>original: *ir-ri-šum*</note> then produces grain or sesame in that field, at the time of the <term>harvest: *ebūrum*, the season of gathering crops</term>, it is the owner of the field who shall take the grain or sesame that is produced in the field. He shall then give to the merchant grain in exchange for the money he borrowed, along with its interest, and he shall also compensate the merchant for the <term>costs of cultivation: *ma-nāḫāt*, referring to the labor and expenses of the farming work</term>.

### § 50.—XIV, 45-55.

¶ If the field he gives [to the merchant] was already a planted grain field or a planted sesame field, it is the owner of the field who shall take the grain or sesame produced in that field; he shall then return the money and its interest to the merchant.

### § 51.—XIV, 56-66.

¶ If he does not have the money to repay his debt, he shall instead give to the merchant sesame—at its market value—to cover the money and its interest which he received from the merchant, according to the <term>royal ordinance: *ṣimdat šarrim*, a standard price or interest rate set by the king</term> to regulate the economy.

### § 52.—XV, 1-6.

¶ If the tenant farmer does not produce grain or sesame in the field, he may not alter his contract <note>The debtor remains responsible for the loan even if the harvest fails due to poor farming.</note>.

### § 53.—XV, 7-20.

¶ If a man is too lazy to strengthen the <term>dike: *kārum*, the embankment or bank of an irrigation canal</term> of his field, and he does not strengthen it, and a breach then opens in his dike so that the water carries away the crops of the <term>communal field: *ugaram*, the shared farmland of the village</term>, the man in whose dike the breach occurred shall replace the grain that was destroyed <note>The law here emphasizes communal responsibility; a single farmer’s negligence could ruin the entire neighborhood’s food supply.</note>.

### § 49.

¶ If a man obtains money <note>original: "silver" (*kaspum*)</note> from a <term>merchant: a *tamkarum*, who functioned as both a state-regulated financier and a trader</term> and gives the merchant a field ready for planting with grain or sesame as <term>security: collateral for a loan</term>, and says to him: "Cultivate the field, and harvest and take for yourself the grain and sesame that is produced;" if the <term>tenant: the farmer hired to work the land</term> then raises grain or sesame in the field, at the time of the harvest, it is the owner of the field who shall take the grain and sesame that is in the field. He shall then give to the merchant grain in exchange for the money he borrowed, along with its interest and the costs for the <term>maintenance: the expenses incurred for labor and upkeep</term> of the tenant.

### § 50.

¶ If he gives as security a field already planted with grain or a field already planted with sesame, the owner of the field shall still receive the grain or the sesame produced in that field, and he shall return the loan and its interest to the merchant.

### § 51.

¶ If he does not have the money to repay the loan, he shall instead give to the merchant grain or sesame to cover the value of the loan and its interest, according to the <term>royal ordinance: *ṣimdat šarrim*, a standard price or exchange rate fixed by the king</term> to prevent the exploitation of debtors.

### § 52.

¶ If the tenant farmer does not succeed in producing a crop of grain or sesame in his field, he shall not cancel his contract <note>The obligation to the merchant remains, as the failure to produce a crop does not necessarily void the underlying debt or the agreement to farm the land</note>.

### § 53.

¶ If a man is negligent in maintaining his <term>dyke: an embankment (*īkum*) designed to manage irrigation water</term> and does not reinforce it, and a breach occurs in his dyke so that the escaping water carries away the soil of the <term>farm-land: the *ugārum*, or communal field area</term>, the man in whose dyke the breach occurred shall replace the grain that was destroyed <note>This law establishes "strict liability" for infrastructure; the owner is responsible for damages caused to his neighbors by his failure to maintain irrigation works</note>.

### § 54.—XV, 21-30.

¶ If he is unable to replace the grain, he and his possessions shall be sold for silver, and the <term>members of the village district: *mārū ugārim*, the fellow farmers sharing the communal irrigation area</term> whose grain the water carried away shall divide the proceeds. <note>This law establishes communal restitution; if a farmer's negligence ruins his neighbors' crops and he is insolvent, his entire estate is liquidated to compensate the community.</note>

### § 55.—XV, 31-38.

¶ If a man opens his <term>irrigation ditch: *atappum*</term> to water his crop but is careless, and the water floods the field of his neighbor, he shall measure out grain to his neighbor in proportion to the neighboring yields. <note>The phrase "is careless" literally translates to "lets his arm drop" (*ahšu iddima*), implying a failure to maintain the dikes.</note>

### § 56.—XV, 39-45.

¶ If a man releases water and thereby floods the <term>cultivated works: *ipšētim*, referring to the labor and seed already invested in the land</term> of his neighbor’s field, he shall measure out <term>ten GUR of grain: approximately 3,000 liters</term> for every <term>ten GAN of land: approximately 3.5 hectares</term>.

### § 57.—XV, 46-64.

¶ If a shepherd has not reached an agreement with the owner of a field to graze sheep, and yet without the owner's permission he lets the sheep graze on the field, the owner shall harvest his own field, and the shepherd who let the sheep graze on the field without the owner's permission shall give, in addition, <term>twenty GUR of grain per ten GAN</term> to the owner of the field.

### § 58.—XV, 65—XVI, 3.

¶ If, after the sheep have come up from the <term>communal pasture: *ugarum*</term> and the <term>emblem of the season's end: *kannu gamartim*, a signal or barrier marking the official end of the grazing period</term> has been wound around the city gate, a shepherd then turns the sheep into a field and lets them graze there, the shepherd shall take charge of the field he has allowed them to graze upon, and at the time of harvest, he shall measure out <term>sixty GUR of grain per ten GAN</term> to the owner of the field. <note>The penalty here is much higher—three times the rate of the previous law—because the offense occurs after the grazing season has officially closed, implying willful trespass.</note>

### § 59.—XVI, 4-9.

¶ If a man, without the permission of the owner of an orchard, cuts down a tree in another man’s orchard, he shall pay <term>one-half mina of silver: approximately 250 grams, a substantial fine</term>.

### § 54.

¶ If he is not able to replace the grain <note>original: "restore the grain"</note>, he and his possessions shall be sold for silver, and the <term>fellow farmers: *mārū ugārim*, literally "sons of the irrigation district"</term> whose grain the water carried away shall divide the proceeds of the sale. <note>This law ensures that if a single farmer's negligence destroys the community's food supply and he cannot pay the debt, his entire status as a free man is forfeit to compensate his neighbors.</note>

### § 55.

¶ If a man opens his <term>irrigation canal: *atappum*</term> for watering and is negligent, so that the water carries away the soil of an adjacent field, he shall measure out grain to his neighbor based on the yields produced by the neighboring fields.

### § 56.

¶ If a man releases water and the water carries away the <term>planted crops: *ipšētim*, referring to the labor and seed already invested</term> of an adjacent field, he shall measure out <term>ten GUR: approximately 3,000 liters</term> of grain for every <term>ten GAN: approximately 3.5 hectares</term> of land.

### § 57.

¶ If a shepherd has not reached an agreement with the owner of a field to graze sheep on the grass, and he lets the sheep graze on the field without the owner's permission, the owner shall still harvest his own field, but the shepherd who grazed his sheep there without permission must give an additional <term>twenty GUR of grain per ten GAN</term> to the owner of the field. <note>This penalty is a "top-off" payment to compensate for the reduced yield caused by the animals eating the young sprouts.</note>

### § 58.

¶ If, after the sheep have come up from the <term>meadow: *rītum*</term> and have passed through the <term>city gate: *kānum*</term> to the common pasture, the shepherd then turns the sheep back into a field and grazes them there, that shepherd shall take over the management of the field he damaged. At the time of harvest, he must measure out a heavy penalty of <term>sixty GUR of grain per ten GAN</term> to the owner of the field. <note>The significantly higher penalty here (60 GUR vs 20 GUR) reflects the deliberate nature of the trespass after the grazing season has officially ended.</note>

### § 59.

¶ If a man cuts down a tree in another man’s orchard without the owner's permission, he shall pay <term>one-half mana of silver: approximately 250 grams</term>. <note>Silver was the standard for high-value fines; half a mana was a substantial sum, reflecting the long-term investment required to grow fruit-bearing trees.</note>

### § 60. — XVI, 10-26.

¶ If a man gives a field to a <term>gardener: *nukaribbum*</term> to plant as an <term>orchard: *kirûm*, typically referring to a date palm grove</term>, and the gardener plants the orchard and cares for it for four years; in the fifth year, the owner of the orchard and the gardener shall divide the yield equally <note>original: *mithariš izuzzū*, meaning "they shall divide into equal parts"</note>. The owner of the orchard shall choose and take his share first.

### § 61. — XVI, 27-33.

¶ If the gardener, while planting the orchard, does not complete the work and leaves a <term>waste area: *nidītum*, a fallow or unplanted plot</term>, the gardener shall have that waste area included within his own share. <note>This law prevents the gardener from neglecting difficult soil or leaving gaps in the grove while still claiming a full half of the productive trees.</note>

### § 62. — XVI, 34-47.

¶ If he does not plant the field which was given to him as an orchard, but it is <term>arable land: *abšênum*, literally "furrow-work"</term>, the gardener shall measure out to the owner of the field the grain yield of the field for the years it was neglected, according to the yields produced by his neighbors; he shall perform the necessary work on the field and return it to the owner.

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI

### § 60. — XVI, 10–26.

¶ If a man gives a field to a <term>gardener: *nukaribbum*</term> to plant as an <term>orchard: *kirûm*, specifically a date-palm grove</term>, and the gardener plants the orchard and cares for it for four years; in the fifth year, the owner of the orchard and the gardener shall share the yield equally. The owner of the orchard shall choose and take his portion first. <note>In ancient Mesopotamia, date palms took about five years to reach significant productivity. This law provides a "grace period" for the gardener to establish the trees before the owner begins taking half the profit.</note>

### § 61. — XVI, 27–33.

¶ If the gardener does not finish planting the whole field, but leaves a <term>waste area: *nidītum*, an uncultivated or empty plot</term>, that waste area shall be assigned to the gardener as part of his share. <note>This penalty ensures the gardener is held accountable for the entire plot of land entrusted to him; he cannot avoid work on difficult sections and still claim half of the good trees.</note>

### § 62. — XVI, 34–47.

¶ If he does not plant the field which was given to him as an orchard, but it was <term>arable land: *abšênum*, land prepared for grain</term>, the gardener shall measure out to the owner of the field the grain produce of the field for the years it was neglected, based on the yield of the neighboring fields; he shall perform the necessary labor on the field to restore it and then return it to the owner. <note>The Law uses neighbors’ crops as a "fair market value" benchmark to prevent the owner from losing income due to the gardener's failure to convert the land.</note>

### § 63. — XVI, 48–57.

¶ If the land was <term>unreclaimed: *KI.KAL*, virgin or long-fallow soil</term>, he shall perform the required work on the field and return it to the owner; for each year of neglect, he shall measure out <term>ten GUR: approximately 3,000 liters</term> of grain for every <term>ten GAN: approximately 35 hectares or 86 acres</term>.

### § 64. — XVI, 58–70.

¶ If a man gives his established orchard to a gardener to manage, the gardener shall give the owner of the orchard two-thirds of the produce of the orchard for as long as he holds it; he shall keep one-third for himself. <note>For an established orchard where the heavy labor of planting is already done, the "rent" or share for the owner increases from 50% to 66%.</note>

### § 65. — XVI, 71–77.

¶ If the gardener does not manage the orchard properly and causes the yield to diminish, the gardener shall measure out a share of the produce based on the yields of the adjacent orchards. <note>This protects the landowner from a lazy or incompetent sharecropper, ensuring the "two-thirds" share is based on the land's potential, not just the gardener's poor results.</note>

<summary>This section of the Code outlines the contractual obligations for date palm cultivation, establishing a 50/50 split for new groves and a 2/3 share for established ones, while penalizing negligence with local yield benchmarks.</summary>

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI

### § 100.—XVII, 1-7.

¶ . . . XVII, 1. [He shall write down] the interest on the money, 2. as much as he has received, 3. and he shall record it in order; 4. he shall count up 5. his days, 6. and he shall pay 7. his <term>merchant: *tamkarum*</term>. <note>This section describes the standard accounting procedure for a traveling agent. In Babylon, business was conducted on credit, and the agent was required to keep a chronological log of interest and time spent on the journey to settle accounts fairly.</note>

### § 101.—XVII, 8-14.

8. If, in the place 9. where he has gone, 10. he has not found 11. a profit, 12. he shall double the money he received 13. and the <term>agent: *šamallûm*</term> 14. shall give it to the merchant. <note>The *šamallûm* was a junior partner or agent. This law implies that if the failure to profit was due to the agent's poor management (rather than bad luck or theft), he was liable to return double the principal to protect the merchant's investment.</note>

### § 102.—XVII, 15-23.

15. If a merchant 16. has given to an agent 17. money as a <term>favor: *tadmiqtum*</term>, 18. and 19. in the place where he has gone 20. he has experienced 21. a loss, 22. he shall return the <term>principal: *qaqqad*, literally "head"</term> of the money 23. to the merchant. <note>A *tadmiqtum* was an interest-free loan intended to help an agent get started or to perform a specific task. Because the merchant took a risk to show "favor," the agent is only required to pay back the original amount if the venture fails, rather than the doubled penalty in § 101.</note>

### § 103.—XVII, 24-31.

24. If, while he is 25. on a journey, 26. an enemy 27. causes him to give up 28. anything that he was carrying, 29. the agent 30. shall swear an <term>oath by the god: *nīš ilim*</term> 31. and he shall be released from obligation. <note>This is an early form of "force majeure" or insurance. If the loss was due to an "Act of God" or a robber (enemy) beyond his control, the agent was not held liable, provided he swore a sacred oath of his innocence.</note>

### § 104.—XVII, 32-45.

32. If a merchant 33. gives to an agent 34. grain, wool, oil, 35. or any other 36. goods 37. to sell, 38. the agent 39. shall record the money [the proceeds] 40. and return it 41. to the merchant; 42. the agent 43. shall receive 44. a <term>sealed receipt: *kanikum*</term> for the money 45. which he gives to the merchant.

### § 105.—XVII, 46-54.

46. If the agent 47. is careless 48. and the sealed receipt 49. for the money 50. he gave 51. to the merchant 52. he does not take, 53. money without a sealed receipt 54. shall not be placed in the <term>account: *nikkassum*</term>. <note>The Babylonian legal system relied heavily on physical evidence. If an agent handed over cash but forgot to get a clay tablet receipt (the *kanikum*), the law refused to recognize the payment, effectively forcing the agent to pay twice. This enforced strict record-keeping.</note>

### § 106.—XVII, 55-67.

55. If an agent 56. has received money 57. from a merchant 58. and then 59. disputes it with his merchant, 60. that merchant... <note>The text continues on the next page/column, likely detailing the legal process for a merchant to sue an agent who denies receiving investment capital.</note>

### § 100.

¶ . . . XVII, 1. [He shall write down] 2. the interest on the money, 3. as much as he has received; 4. he shall record it in order; 5. he shall count up 6. his days, 7. and he shall pay his <term>merchant: *tamkarum*</term>. <note>This law establishes the standard for Babylonian commercial accounting. Traveling agents were required to maintain a chronological ledger of both the time spent and the interest accrued on the merchant's capital to ensure a fair settlement upon their return.</note>

### § 101.

¶ 8. If, in the place 9. where he has gone, 10. he has not found 11. a profit, 12. he shall double the money he received 13. and the <term>agent: *šamallûm*</term> 14. shall give it to the merchant. <note>The *šamallûm* acted as a junior partner or apprentice. This penalty suggests that if the failure to generate profit was due to the agent's poor management or lack of effort, he was personally liable to protect the merchant’s investment from loss.</note>

### § 102.

¶ 15. If a merchant 16. has given to an agent 17. money as a <term>favor: *tadmiqtum*</term>, 18. and 19. in the place where he has gone 20. he has experienced 21. a loss, 22. he shall return the <term>principal: *qaqqad*, literally "head"</term> of the money 23. to the merchant. <note>A *tadmiqtum* was an interest-free loan given out of goodwill. Because the merchant waived the interest to show "favor," the agent is only required to return the original sum if the business venture fails, rather than paying the double penalty described in the previous law.</note>

### § 103.

¶ 24. If, while he is 25. on a journey, 26. an enemy 27. causes him to give up 28. anything he was carrying, 29. the agent 30. shall take an oath 31. by the name of God 32. and he shall be acquitted. <note>original: *itamma-ma utaššar*. This is a "force majeure" clause. If an agent is robbed by bandits or enemies, he is cleared of his debt provided he swears a ritual oath in a temple, proving he did not embezzle the goods himself.</note>

### § 104.

¶ 33. If a merchant 34. has given to an agent 35. grain, wool, oil 36. or any other goods 37. for trade, 38. the agent 39. shall write down the value 40. and return [the money] to the merchant. 41. The agent 42. shall receive 43. a sealed <term>receipt: *kunukkum*</term> 44. for the money 45. which he gives to the merchant. <note>Babylonian law relied heavily on physical evidence. ### § 107.

### § 112.—XVIII, 50-74.

### § 113.—XVIII, 75-XIX, 16.

### § 114.—XIX, 17-25.

### § 116.—XIX, 38-53.

38 If a 38 distress-hostage 42 dies 39 in the house of the 39 distrainer 40 from 40 blows 41 or from 41 ill-treatment; 43 the owner of the 43 distress-hostage 45 shall convict 44 his merchant; 46 if the hostage was 46 the son of a citizen, 47 they shall kill his son... <note>This is a classic example of *lex talionis* (eye-for-an-eye) in Hammurabi's Code. ### § 112.

¶ If a man is on a journey and gives silver, gold, precious stones, or portable property to another man with a commission for transportation, and if that man does not deliver those goods to the intended destination but instead keeps them for himself <note>This law addresses embezzlement by a carrier. In the Babylonian economy, where trade routes were long and dangerous, trust in a "commissioner" was vital for the functioning of the state.</note>, the owner of the goods shall call that man to account for the property which he failed to deliver. That man shall then pay the owner five times the value of the goods given to him.

---

### § 113.

¶ If a man is owed a debt of grain or money by another, and if he takes grain from the heap or the granary without the owner's consent, they shall call that man to account for taking the grain illegally. He shall return exactly as much grain as he took, and he shall forfeit the entirety of the original loan, whatever its value may have been. <note>This statute prevents "self-help" debt collection. Even if a debt was validly owed, a creditor could not simply seize assets without a legal order; doing so resulted in the loss of the debt itself.</note>

---

### § 114.

¶ If a man is not actually owed a debt of grain or money by another, yet he seizes him <note>The practice of "seizure" involved taking a person (often a family member or slave of the debtor) as a hostage to force repayment.</note> for debt, he shall pay a fine of one-third <term>mana</term> <note>A Babylonian unit of weight; one-third of a mana is approximately 170 grams of silver.</note> of silver for each such seizure.

---

### § 115.

¶ If a man is owed a debt of grain or money, and he seizes a person for that debt, and the person seized dies a natural death in the house of the one who seized them, that case carries no legal penalty.

---

### § 116.

¶ If the person seized dies from abuse or neglect while in the house of the one who seized them, the owner of the seized person shall call the merchant <note>Here, "merchant" refers to the creditor who initiated the seizure.</note> to account. If the person who died was the son of a man, they <note>The law likely concludes with "shall put his [the creditor's] son to death," reflecting the *Lex Talionis* or "eye for an eye" principle found elsewhere in the Code.</note>

### § 137.

¶ If a man <term>awīlum</term> <note>original: "a-wi-lum"; a member of the upper class of free citizens.</note> sets his face to divorce a concubine <term>šalšugitum</term> who has borne him children, or a wife who has provided him with children, he shall return her dowry <term>šeriktum</term> <note>The property a bride brings from her father’s house to her new household.</note> to her. Additionally, they shall give her a portion of the field, the garden, and the goods, so that she may raise her children. After she has raised her children, they shall give her a portion equal to that of one heir from whatever was given to her children. She may then marry the man of her heart <note>The law provides economic independence to a divorced mother, allowing her to remarry once her children are grown.</note>.

### § 138.

¶ If a man divorces his first wife <note>original: "ḫīrtu"; the primary or legal wife.</note> who has not borne him children, he shall give her silver in the amount of her bride-price <term>tirḫatu</term> <note>The payment made by the groom to the bride's father to seal the marriage contract.</note>. He shall also make whole for her the dowry which she brought from her father's house, and then he may divorce her.

### § 139.

¶ If there was no bride-price, he shall give her one mina <note>A unit of weight; one mina of silver was a substantial sum, roughly 60 shekels.</note> of silver as a divorce settlement.

### § 140.

¶ If he is a commoner <term>Muskenum</term> <note>original: "MAŠ.EN.KAK"; a social class below the full citizen (awīlum) but above the slave.</note>, he shall give her one-third of a mina of silver.

### § 141.

¶ If a man's wife, while living in the man's house, sets her face to go out and misappropriates goods <note>original: "zikiltam izakkil"; refers to acting recklessly with household resources or secretly hoarding assets.</note>, wastes her house, or belittles her husband, they shall prosecute her. If her husband declares "I divorce her," he may let her go; her way is free, but nothing shall be given to her as a divorce settlement. If her husband declares "I do not divorce her," her husband may marry another woman, and that first woman shall dwell in the house of her husband as a slave <term>amtu</term>.

It also establishes the legal penalties for a wife who neglects her household duties or disrespects her husband.</summary>

### § 137.

¶ If a man <term>awīlum</term> <note>original: "a-wi-lum"; a member of the elite free class.</note> determines to divorce a concubine who has borne him children, or a wife who has provided him with children, he must return her dowry <term>šeriktum</term> <note>The property or money a bride's family provides at the time of marriage.</note> to her. Furthermore, he shall grant her the usage of a field, a garden, and other property so that she may provide for her children. Once she has raised her children, they shall give her a portion of the inheritance equal to that of a single son. Afterward, she is free to marry the man of her choice <note>This law ensures that a mother is financially supported while raising her children and retains her personal agency once they reach adulthood.</note>.

### § 138.

¶ If a man wishes to divorce his primary wife <note>original: "ḫīrtu"; the legal, first-ranking wife.</note> who has not borne him children, he must pay her silver equal to the value of her marriage settlement <term>tirḫatu</term> <note>The "bride-price" paid by the groom to the bride's father to seal the contract.</note>. He must also return the dowry she brought from her father's house in its entirety; only then may he divorce her.

### § 139.

¶ If there was no formal marriage settlement <note>In cases where no "bride-price" was paid at the start of the marriage.</note>, he shall pay her one mina <note>A significant weight of silver, approximately 500 grams or 60 shekels.</note> of silver as a divorce fine.

### § 140.

¶ If the man is a commoner <term>muškēnum</term> <note>A free citizen of a lower social tier than the elite awīlum.</note>, he shall pay her one-third of a mina of silver.

### § 141.

¶ If a man’s wife, who is living in his house, decides to behave recklessly <note>original: "wa-ṣi-a-at"; literally "to go out," implying neglect of domestic duties or behaving indiscreetly in public.</note>, neglects her household, and disparages her husband, they shall bring her to legal account. If her husband formally declares, "I divorce her," he may let her go, but she shall receive no silver or settlement for the divorce. However, if her husband says, "I do not divorce her," he may take another woman as his wife, and the first wife shall remain in his house as a servant <term>amtu</term>.

<summary>These laws outline the financial protections for divorced women, which vary based on whether they have children and their husband's social status, while also establishing harsh penalties for wives who neglect their domestic responsibilities.</summary>

### § 142.—XXIII, 60—XXIV, 5.

If a woman <term>zinništum</term> <note>original: "zinništum"; a general term for a woman or wife.</note> hates her husband and has declared: "You shall not possess me," her past conduct shall be investigated by her district council <term>babtum</term> <note>original: "ba-ab-ti-ša"; the local neighborhood or city ward that acted as a local court to verify social behavior.</note>. If she has been circumspect <note>original: "na-aṣ-ra-at"; meaning she has been careful, chaste, or observant of her duties.</note> and has no fault, but her husband has been going out and greatly belittling her, that woman bears no guilt. She shall take her dowry <term>šeriktum</term> <note>The property her father provided at her marriage.</note> and return to her father’s house.

---

### § 143.—XXIV, 6-12.

If she has not been circumspect, but has been gadabout <note>original: "wa-zi-a-at"; literally "one who goes out," implying neglect of the home or improper behavior.</note>, wasting her household and belittling her husband, they shall throw that woman into the water <note>A common Babylonian capital punishment, typically involving drowning in the river.</note>.

---

### § 144.—XXIV, 13-27.

If a man <term>awīlum</term> <note>A member of the free, upper class.</note> marries a wife, and that wife gives a maidservant to her husband and she <note>the maidservant</note> bears children, but that man then sets his face to marry a concubine <term>šugītum</term> <note>A "shugitum" was a secondary wife, often of a specific social or religious class, who could bear children.</note>, they shall not permit that man his wish; he shall not marry a concubine.

---

### § 145.—XXIV, 28-42.

If a man marries a wife and she does not provide him with children, and he sets his face to marry a concubine, that man may marry the concubine and bring her into his house. However, that concubine shall not be made equal in rank with the primary wife.

---

### § 146.—XXIV, 43-59.

If a man marries a wife and she gives a maidservant to her husband and she bears children, and afterward that maidservant attempts to rank herself with her mistress <note>original: "be-el-ti-ša"; her lady or female owner.</note> because she bore children, her mistress may not sell her for silver. She may, however, mark her with the slave-mark <term>abbuttutum</term> <note>original: "ab-bu-ut-tam"; a distinctive mark or hairstyle that identified a person’s servile status.</note> and count her among the maidservants.

### **§ 142.**

¶ If a woman hates her husband and has declared: “You shall not possess me,” the authorities shall investigate her past conduct to see if she has any faults. ### **§ 143.**

### **§ 144.**

¶ If a man marries a wife and that wife gives a maidservant to her husband and she bears children; if that man then intends to take a concubine <term>šugītum</term> <note>A "shugitum" was a secondary wife of lower social status, often brought in to ensure the lineage continued.</note>, they shall not permit him to do so. ### **§ 145.**

¶ If a man marries a wife and she does not provide him with children, and he intends to take a concubine, that man may take a concubine and bring her into his house. However, that concubine shall not rank equally with his wife.

### **§ 146.**

¶ If a man marries a wife and she gives a maidservant to her husband, and that maidservant bears children and afterwards attempts to claim equal rank with her mistress because she has borne children, her mistress may not sell her for money. Instead, she may reduce her to bondage <note>Literally returning her to the status of a common slave, often involving a physical mark of servitude.</note> and count her among the maidservants.

### § 147.—XXIV, 60–64.

¶ If she <note>The maidservant referred to in the previous sections, who was reduced back to slavery for her arrogance.</note> has not borne children, her mistress may sell her for silver.

### § 148.—XXIV, 65–81.

¶ If a man marries a wife and a chronic skin disease <term>la’bum</term> <note>original: "la-’a-bu-um"; interpreted as a serious, debilitating, or perhaps contagious illness that could justify a man taking a second wife while still requiring him to care for the first.</note> seizes her, and he sets his face to marry another woman, he may marry her. ### § 149.—XXV, 1–9.

### § 150.—XXV, 10–25.

¶ If a man bestows a field, garden, house, or goods upon his wife and leaves her a sealed deed <term>kunukkum</term> <note>A legal document impressed with a cylinder seal to ensure its validity.</note> for it; after her husband’s death, her children may not bring a claim against her. ### § 151.—XXV, 26–51.

Furthermore, if that woman had a debt upon her before she entered the man’s house, her creditors may not seize her husband.

### § 151.

¶ If a woman who dwells in the house of a man makes a contract with her husband that a creditor of his may not seize her for his debts, and she compels him to deliver a written agreement; if that man had a debt before he took that woman, his creditor may not seize his wife. Furthermore, if that woman had a debt before she entered the man’s house, her creditor may not seize her husband. <note>This law functions as a pre-nuptial agreement, protecting individual property from the partner’s pre-existing financial failures.</note>
