¶ If a man has "known" <note>a common euphemism for sexual relations</note> his daughter, they shall expel that man from the city.

### § 155.—XXV, 72—XXVI, 1.

¶ If a man has betrothed a bride <term>kallâtam</term> <note>original: "kallâtam"; specifically a daughter-in-law chosen by a father for his son.</note> for his son, and his son has known her; if the father himself afterward lies in her bosom and they catch him, they shall bind that man and throw her <note>original: "i-na-ad-du-u-ši"; while the man is bound, the text specifies casting "her" into the water, though many legal scholars suggest this implies both parties or refers back to the man via a scribal variant.</note> into the water.

### § 156.—XXVI, 2-17.

¶ If a man has betrothed a bride for his son, but his son has not yet known her, and he himself lies in her bosom, he shall pay to her one-half mana of silver <note>A significant fine; a mana was roughly 500 grams, so this is about 250 grams of silver.</note>. Furthermore, he shall make good to her whatever she brought from her father's house, and the husband of her heart <note>original: "mu-tu li-ib-bi-ša"; a man of her own choosing.</note> may marry her.

### § 157.—XXVI, 18-23.

¶ If a man, after his father’s death, lies in the bosom of his mother, they shall burn both of them together.

### § 158.—XXVI, 24-32.

¶ If a man, after his father’s death, is caught in the bosom of his "chief mother" <note>original: "ra-bi-ti-šu"; referring to the father’s primary wife who is not the man's biological mother.</note> who has borne children, that man shall be cut off <note>original: "in-na-az-za-aḫ"</note> from his father’s house.

### § 159.

¶ If a man, who has brought a **ceremonial gift** <term>biblam</term> <note>original: "biblam"; a gift brought by the groom to the bride's father to seal the engagement.</note> to the house of his father-in-law and has given the **bride-price** <term>tirḥatam</term> <note>original: "tirḥatam"; a sum paid by the groom's family to the bride's father, often used to help set up the new household.</note>, then looks with longing upon another woman and says to his father-in-law, “I will not marry your daughter;” the father of the daughter shall take and keep for himself whatever was brought to him.

### § 160.

¶ If a man brings a ceremonial gift to the house of his father-in-law and gives a bride-price, and the father of the daughter then says, “I will not give you my daughter;” he *(meaning the father-in-law)* shall double the amount of everything that was brought to him and return it to the man.

### § 161.

¶ If a man brings a ceremonial gift to the house of his father-in-law and gives a bride-price, and his friend then **slanders him** <note>original: "ug-dar-ri-zu"; to speak maliciously or bring false accusations in order to sabotage the man's reputation.</note>; and if his father-in-law, influenced by this, says to the prospective husband, “You shall not have my daughter,” the father-in-law shall double the amount of everything that was brought to him and return it. Furthermore, the friend who spoke the slander shall not be allowed to marry the woman. <note>This law prevents a treacherous friend from profiting or benefiting from the broken engagement he caused.</note>

### § 162.

¶ If a man takes a wife and she bears him children, and that woman then dies, her father may not lay claim to her **dowry** <term>šeriktum</term> <note>original: "šeriktum"; the property or money brought by the bride from her own father's house into the marriage.</note>. Her dowry belongs to her children.

### § 163.

¶ If a man takes a wife and she does not bear him children, and that woman then dies; if his father-in-law returns to him the **bride-price** that the man originally brought to the house of his father-in-law, the husband may not lay claim to the **dowry** of that woman. In this case, her dowry belongs to her father’s house. <note>This ensures that if no children were produced to inherit the woman's family wealth, and the groom's initial "investment" is returned, the family property stays within the bride's original lineage.</note>

### § 164.

If his father-in-law does not return the **bride-price** <term>tirḫatam</term> <note>A payment made by the groom to the bride's father to seal the engagement.</note> to him, he may deduct the full amount of that bride-price from her **dowry** <term>šeriktum</term> <note>The property or money a woman brings from her father's home into her marriage.</note> and then return the remainder of her dowry to her father’s house.

### § 165.

If a man grants a field, garden, or house to his favorite son—the one who is **pleasing in his eyes**—and provides him with a **sealed deed** <term>kunukkam</term>; after the father has **gone to his fate** <note>A standard Mesopotamian euphemism for death.</note>, when the brothers divide the inheritance, the favorite son shall first take the specific gift his father gave him. After that, they shall all divide the remaining property of the father’s house equally among themselves.

### § 166.

If a man has provided wives for his older sons but has not yet provided a wife for his youngest son; after the father dies, when the brothers divide the estate, they must set aside money for a **bride-price** <term>tirḫatam</term> from the father's goods for their younger brother in addition to his regular share. They shall then enable him to take a wife.

### § 167.

If a man takes a wife and she bears him children, and after she dies he takes a second wife who also bears him children; when the father eventually dies, the children shall not simply divide the entire estate together. Instead, the children of the first wife shall receive their mother’s **dowry** <term>šeriktum</term>, and the children of the second wife shall receive their mother's dowry. However, they shall all divide the property of the father’s house equally.

### § 168.

If a man is determined to **disinherit** <note>To formally and legally strip a child of their right to inherit the family property.</note> his son and declares to the judges, "I wish to disinherit my son," the judges shall first inquire into the facts of the case...

<note>original: "mâri-i a-na-za-aḫ biḳ-ta-bi"</note> ...if he says, "I will disinherit my son," the **judges** <term>dayyānu</term> shall examine his **past record** <note>original: "warkazu", meaning his history or the circumstances of the case</note>. If the son has not committed a **grave crime** <term>arnam kabtam</term> which warrants **disinheritance** <term>ablūtim nasāḫim</term> <note>Literally "tearing out from the status of heir."</note>, the father may not disinherit his son.

### § 169.—XXVIII, 25-37.

If he has committed a **grave crime** against his father which warrants disinheritance, for the **first offense** <note>original: "ana ištiššu"</note> the judges shall **grant him a pardon** <note>original: "pānišu ubbalu", an idiom meaning to overlook the offense or show favor.</note>. If he commits a **grave crime** for a **second time** <note>original: "adi šinīšu"</note>, the father may indeed **disinherit** his son.

### § 170.—XXVIII, 38-60.

If a man’s **first-rank wife** <term>ḫirtu</term> <note>The primary legal wife, often of similar social standing to the husband.</note> bears him children, and his **slave-woman** <term>amtu</term> also bears him children, and the father during his lifetime says to the children whom the slave-woman bore him, "**They are my children**," and thus counts them among the children of the first-rank wife; after the father has **gone to his fate** <note>Died.</note>, the children of the first-rank wife and the children of the slave-woman shall **divide the property** of the paternal estate **equally** <note>original: "mitḫāriš".</note>. The **firstborn son** <term>mārum aplum</term> <note>The eldest son of the primary wife typically received a larger or preferred share.</note> of the first-rank wife shall choose and take his share first.

### § 171.—XXVIII, 61—XXIX, 5.

If, however, the father during his lifetime **did not say** "They are my children" to the children the slave-woman bore him; after the father has gone to his fate, the children of the slave-woman **shall not share** in the property of the paternal estate with the children of the first-rank wife. Instead, the **freedom** <term>andurārum</term> <note>A legal release from debt or servitude; manumission.</note> of the slave-woman and her children shall be established. The children of the first-rank wife **may not lay claim** to the children of the slave-woman for **slavery**. 

The **first-rank wife** shall take her **dowry** <term>šeriktum</term> and any **gift** <term>nudunnûm</term> <note>A specific settlement or property gift given by a husband to his wife during the marriage.</note> that her husband gave to her and recorded for her in a **sealed deed** <note>original: "dubbum", a clay tablet.</note>. She may live in the **dwelling of her husband** and utilize it <column-break/> as long as she lives. She **may not sell** it for silver. After her death, her property belongs only to **her own children**.

### § 169.

### § 171.

The **maid servant** and her children shall be **given their freedom** <note>While they do not inherit property, they are legally manumitted (freed) upon the father's death.</note>. The children of the wife may not **lay claim** to the children of the maid servant for service. The wife shall receive her **dowry** <term>šeriḳtum</term> and the **settlement** <term>nudunnū</term> <note>A gift or marital settlement deeded by the husband to the wife.</note> which her husband gave and deeded to her on a **tablet** and she may dwell in the house of her husband and enjoy the property as long as she lives. She **cannot sell it**, however, for after her death it belongs to her children.

### § 172.—XXIX, 6–26.

¶ If her husband did not give her a **marriage settlement** <term>nudunnûm</term> <note>A gift given by a husband to his wife during the marriage, distinct from the dowry she brought from her father.</note>, they shall make good her **dowry** <term>šeriktum</term> <note>The property a woman brings from her father's house into her marriage.</note> for her, and she shall take a portion from the **goods** of her husband’s house equal to that of **one heir** <note>original: "kīma ablim ištēn", meaning she receives a share of the estate equivalent to what one of the sons would inherit.</note>. If her children **harass** <note>original: "uzahhamuši", meaning to press, annoy, or attempt to evict.</note> her in order to drive her out of the house, the **judges** shall investigate her **past record** <note>original: "warkaza", looking into her conduct and the circumstances of the case.</note>, and if they find the children to be at fault, they shall impose a **penalty** <term>arnum</term> upon the children. That woman shall **not go out** from her husband’s house.

### § 172A.—XXIX, 27–40.

¶ If that woman **sets her face to leave** <note>An idiom meaning she intends to move out or remarry.</note>, she shall leave the **marriage settlement** which her husband gave her to her children; she shall take the **dowry** from her father’s house and may marry the **man of her heart** <note>original: "mut libbiša", a phrase indicating a marriage of her own choosing.</note>.

### § 173.—XXIX, 41–50.

¶ If that woman, where she has entered <note>That is, in her second marriage.</note>, bears children to her **later husband**, and afterwards that woman **dies**, her former and later children shall **divide** her dowry.

### § 174.—XXIX, 51–56.

¶ If she does not bear children to her **later husband**, the children of her **first spouse** <note>original: "hāwirīša", referring to her first husband.</note> shall take her dowry.

### § 175.—XXIX, 57–68.

¶ If either a **palace slave** <term>warad ēkallim</term> or the slave of a **commoner** <term>muškênum</term> <note>original: "MAŠ.EN.KAK", referring to a social class of state-dependents or citizens with fewer rights than the elite 'awīlum' class.</note> marry the **daughter of a free man** <term>mārat awīlim</term> and she bears children, the owner of the slave shall have **no claim** for **servitude** <note>original: "wardūtim", meaning the children cannot be claimed as slaves by the father's master; they are born free.</note> against the children of the daughter of the free man.

### § 172.

¶ If her husband has not given her a **marriage settlement** <term>nudunnûm</term> <note>A gift given by a husband to his wife during the marriage, distinct from the dowry she brought from her father.</note>, they shall restore her **dowry** <term>šeriktum</term> <note>The property a woman brings from her father's house into her marriage.</note> to her, and she shall receive a portion of the goods from her husband’s estate equal to the share of one son. If the woman is determined to leave, she shall leave the **marriage settlement** <note>original: "nudunnûm"</note> which her husband gave her to her children; she may take the **dowry** of her father’s house, and the **husband of her choice** <note>An idiom suggesting she is free to remarry whomever she wishes.</note> may marry her.

### § 173.

If, in the legal deed he has written for her, he has not included the clause "after her death, she may give it to whomever she pleases," and if he has not granted her full discretion over the property; then after her father dies, her brothers shall take possession of her field and garden. However, she may not sell the property or transfer it to another. Her inheritance ultimately belongs to her brothers.

### § 181.—XXXI, 60-75.

If a father has dedicated a **holy woman** <term>kadištum</term> <note>original: *kadištam*; a woman dedicated to a deity, often involved in temple rituals.</note> or a **devotee** <term>NU.PAR</term> <note>A class of temple woman whose specific function is less certain than the nadītum or kadištum.</note> to a god, but has not given her a dowry; after the father **dies** <note>original: *a-na ši-im-tim it-ta-al-ku*; literally "has gone to his fate."</note>, she shall receive a one-third share of a son’s inheritance from the property of the paternal estate. She shall **have the usufruct** <note>original: *i-ik-ka-al*; literally "she shall eat," meaning she may live off the income or produce of the property.</note> of it for as long as she lives. Her estate, however, belongs to her brothers.

### § 182.—XXXI, 76-XXXII, 1.

If a father has a daughter who is a **wife of Marduk of Babylon** <note>Marduk was the patron god of Babylon; his "wives" were high-ranking priestesses who lived in the temple complex.</note> and he has not given her a dowry or a sealed deed; after the father dies, she shall receive a one-third share of a son’s inheritance from the property of the paternal estate along with her brothers. She shall not, however, perform any **feudal service** <term>ilku</term> <note>The *ilku* was a state obligation of labor or military service tied to land ownership.</note>. The wife of Marduk may leave her estate to whomever she **pleases** <note>original: *ṭa-bu*; literally "is good to her." Unlike other priestesses whose property reverted to their brothers, the wives of Marduk had the right to name their own heirs.</note>.

### § 183.—XXXII, 2-14.

If a father has given a dowry to his daughter, a **concubine** <term>šugetum</term> <note>A *šugetum* was a woman of a lower religious or social rank than a *nadītum*, often serving as a secondary wife or lay priestess.</note>, has provided her with a sealed deed, and has given her to a husband; after the father dies, she shall not receive a share of the property of the paternal estate.

### § 184.—XXXII, 15-30.

If a man has not given a dowry to his daughter, a **concubine**, and has not given her to a husband; after the father dies, her brothers shall provide her with a dowry according to the wealth of the paternal estate and shall give her to a husband.

### § 185.—XXXII, 31-38.

If a man takes a young child **to be his son** <note>original: *i-na me-e-šu a-na ma-ru-tim*; literally "from his water [semen] into sonship," a legal formula for formal adoption.</note> and raises him, that child who has been raised may not be reclaimed.

### § 181.

If a father has dedicated a **consecrated woman** <term>votary</term> <note>original: *nadītum*; these were women from elite families dedicated to a god, living in a temple complex or "cloister."</note> or a **temple servant** <term>NU.PAR</term> <note>A specific class of religious woman whose exact duties are less understood than the *nadītum*, but who held distinct legal status.</note> to a god, but has not given her a dowry; after the father **dies** <note>literally "goes to his fate."</note>, she shall receive a one-third share of a son’s inheritance from the property of the paternal estate. She shall have the **usufruct** <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of the property without owning it outright.</note> of it for as long as she lives. After her death, the property belongs to her brothers.

### § 182.

If a father has not given a dowry to his daughter, who is a **priestess of Marduk of Babylon** <note>Marduk was the patron deity of the city of Babylon; his priestesses held exceptionally high social standing and more legal freedom than other religious orders.</note>, and has not written a sealed deed of gift for her; after the father dies, she shall receive a one-third share of a son’s inheritance from the property of the paternal estate along with her brothers. She shall not, however, be required to manage the **business** <note>likely referring to *ilku*, or state-mandated labor and tax obligations tied to the land.</note> of the estate. A priestess of Marduk may leave her property to whomever she **pleases** after her death.

### § 183.

If a father provides a dowry to his daughter, who is a **concubine** <term>shugetum</term> <note>original: *šugetum*; a secondary wife or a class of woman often associated with the temple who was permitted to marry and bear children.</note>, and gives her to a husband and writes a sealed deed for her; after the father dies, she shall not have a further share in the property of the paternal estate.

### § 184.

If a man does not provide a dowry to his daughter, who is a **concubine** <term>shugetum</term>, and does not give her to a husband; after the father dies, her brothers shall provide her a dowry in proportion to the value of the paternal estate and shall find her a husband.

### § 185.

If a man takes a young child **in his name** <note>Meaning a formal, legal adoption where the child takes the father's name.</note> to be his son and rears him, no one may bring a legal claim to demand that adopted son back.

### § 189.

### § 190.

### § 191.

### § 200.

¶ If a **man** <note>original: *awilum*; a member of the upper class or aristocracy.</note> knocks out the tooth of a man of his own rank, they shall knock out his tooth.

### § 201.

¶ If he knocks out the tooth of a **commoner** <term>MAŠ.EN.KAK</term> <note>original: *mushkenum*; a free person of a lower social standing than the elite *awilum*.</note>, he shall pay one-third of a **mina** <term>mana</term> of silver.

### § 202.

¶ If a man strikes the cheek of a man who is his superior in rank, he shall be struck sixty times in the **assembly** <note>original: *puhru*; the public gathering of citizens or elders for judicial purposes.</note> with a whip made of **ox-hide**.

### § 203.

¶ If the son of a man <note>referring again to the elite *awilum* class.</note> strikes the cheek of the son of a man who is his equal, he shall pay one **mina** of silver.

### § 204.

¶ If a commoner strikes the cheek of a commoner, he shall pay ten **shekels** <note>original: *šiqil*; a unit of weight, where 60 shekels equal one mina.</note> of silver.

### § 205.

¶ If a man's slave strikes the cheek of the son of a man <note>an *awilum*.</note>, they shall cut off his ear.

### § 206.

¶ If a man strikes another man in a **quarrel** <note>original: *ina risbatim*; a scuffle or physical confrontation.</note> and causes him a wound, that man shall swear: "I did not strike him intentionally," and he shall pay for the **physician** <term>A.ZU</term> <note>original: *asû*; a doctor or healer. This is one of the earliest legal requirements for a defendant to pay a victim's medical expenses.</note>.

### § 207.

¶ If he dies from the blow, he <note>the striker</note> shall swear [as before]; and if the deceased was the son of a man <note>an *awilum*.</note>, he shall pay one-half **mina** of silver.

### § 208.

¶ If he <note>the deceased</note> was the son of a commoner, he shall pay one-third **mina** of silver.

### § 209.
¶ If a **man** <note>original: *awilum*; a member of the Babylonian upper class.</note> strikes the daughter of another **man** and causes her to lose the fruit of her womb <note>original: *ša libbiša*; literally "that which is in her heart/inside her," referring to a fetus.</note>, he shall pay ten **shekels** <note>original: *šiqil*; one shekel was roughly 8 grams of silver.</note> of silver for her fetus.

### § 210.

#### § 218.—Column XXXIV, lines 73-82.

¶ If a **physician** <term>asû</term> <note>A medical practitioner who performed surgeries and physical treatments.</note> performs a major operation on a **man** <note>original: *awīlum*; a member of the upper class.</note> with a **bronze lancet** <note>original: *GIR.NI siparrim*; a surgical knife made of bronze.</note> and causes the man’s death, or if he opens a man’s **abscess** <note>original: *nagabtum*; possibly a tumor or a growth near the eye.</note> with a bronze lancet and destroys the man’s eye, they shall **cut off his hands** <note>original: *rittē-šu inakkisū*. This reflects the "lex talionis" (law of retaliation) where a professional is physically incapacitated to prevent them from repeating a failed procedure.</note>.

#### § 219.—Column XXXIV, lines 83-87.

¶ If a physician performs a major operation on the **slave of a commoner** <term>mushkēnum</term> <note>A member of the middle social class.</note> with a bronze lancet and causes his death, he shall replace the slave with another slave <note>The penalty for killing a slave is purely economic—replacing property—rather than physical punishment.</note>.

#### § 220.—Column XXXIV, lines 88-93.

¶ If he opens his abscess with a bronze lancet and **destroys his eye**, he shall pay **silver** equal to half of the slave's value <note>original: *kaspam mišil šīmīšu*; half the price of the slave in silver.</note>.

#### § 221.—Column XXXIV, line 94—Column XXXV, line 9.

¶ If a physician heals a man’s **broken bone** or cures a diseased **muscle** <note>original: *šer’ānam*; can refer to a tendon, muscle, or vein.</note>, the patient <note>original: *bēl šimmim*; literally "the master of the ailment."</note> shall give the physician five **shekels** <note>Approximately 40 grams of silver.</note> of silver.

#### § 222.—Column XXXV, lines 10-12.

¶ If it is the son of a **commoner** <term>mushkēnum</term>, he shall give three shekels of silver.

#### § 223.—Column XXXV, lines 13-17.

¶ If it is a man’s **slave**, the owner of the slave shall give the physician two shekels of silver.

#### § 224.—Column XXXV, lines 18-28.

¶ If a **physician of oxen or donkeys** <note>The earliest recorded regulations for veterinary medicine.</note> performs a major operation on an ox or a donkey and cures it, the owner of the ox or donkey shall give the physician one-sixth of a **shekel** of silver as his **fee** <note>original: *ID-šu*; the payment or wage for the service.</note>.

### § 218.

¶ If a **physician** <term>asû</term> <note>A specialized medical practitioner in Babylonian society who focused on surgery and physical remedies.</note> performs a major operation on a **man** <note>original: *awīlum*; a member of the Babylonian aristocracy or upper class.</note> with a **bronze lancet** and causes the man's death, or if he opens an **abscess** <note>original: *nagabtum*; possibly a cataract or a tumor near the eye.</note> in a man's eye with a bronze lancet and destroys the man's eye, they shall **cut off his fingers** <note>original: *rittē-šu inakkisū*. Under the "eye for an eye" principle, the surgeon is physically punished for his failure, which also prevents him from operating again.</note>.

### § 219.

¶ If a physician performs a major operation on the **slave of a commoner** <term>mushkēnum</term> <note>A member of the middle social class who possessed fewer rights than the aristocracy.</note> with a bronze lancet and causes his death, he shall **replace the slave** with another slave of equal value.

### § 220.

¶ If he opens an **abscess** in his eye with a bronze lancet and destroys his eye, he shall pay **silver** to the extent of one-half of the slave's price <note>This payment would be made to the owner of the slave as compensation for the loss of the slave's labor and value.</note>.

### § 221.

¶ If a physician sets a **broken bone** for a man or cures his **diseased bowels**, the patient shall give **five shekels of silver** <note>A shekel was a unit of weight, approximately 8.3 grams. For perspective, a common laborer might earn only 5 to 10 shekels in a full year.</note> to the physician.

### § 222.

¶ If the patient is a **commoner** <note>original: *mār mushkēnim*; literally 'the son of a commoner'.</note>, he shall give **three shekels of silver**.

### § 223.

¶ If it is a man's **slave**, the owner of the slave shall give **two shekels of silver** to the physician.

### § 224.

¶ If a **veterinary physician** <note>original: *asū alpim u imērim*; literally 'a physician of oxen and donkeys'.</note> operates on an ox or a donkey for a severe wound and saves its life, the owner of the ox or donkey shall give to the physician, as his fee, **one-sixth of a shekel of silver**.

### § 225.—XXXV, 29-35.

¶ If a **doctor of oxen or donkeys** <note>Essentially a veterinary surgeon.</note> treats an **ox** or a **donkey** for a **severe wound** <gloss>b</gloss> and causes its death, he shall give **one-fourth** of its value to the owner of the ox <gloss>bu</gloss> or donkey.

### § 226.—XXXV, 36-42.

¶ If a **barber** <term>gallabum</term> <note>Barbers in Babylon often performed minor medical procedures and were responsible for applying or removing the marks of slavery.</note>, without the permission of the **slave's owner**, shaves off the **slave-mark** <term>abbutti</term> <note>A specific hairstyle or brand that identified a person as a slave.</note> of a slave who is not his own, they shall **cut off the hands** <gloss>b</gloss> <note>The text specifies rittē, which can mean hands or fingers; this punishment prevented the barber from practicing his craft.</note> of that barber.

### § 227.—XXXV, 43-55.

¶ If a **man** <term>awīlum</term> <note>A member of the upper class.</note> deceives a barber and causes him to shave off the **slave-mark** of a slave who is not his own, they shall **kill** that man and **hang him** <note>original: *ihallalū-šu*; this could refer to hanging or impalement.</note> at his own gate. The barber shall **swear an oath** <note>A formal testimony before the gods.</note>, saying: "I did not shave him knowingly," and he shall be **set free**.

### § 228.—XXXV, 56-63.

¶ If a **builder** <term>bânûm</term> builds a **house** for a man and **completes it** <gloss>b</gloss>, for every **SAR** <note>A measurement of area, roughly 35 square meters.</note> of the house, the owner shall give him **two shekels of silver** as his fee.

### § 229.—XXXV, 64-72.

¶ If a builder builds a house for a man but does not **make his work strong**, and the house which he built **collapses** and causes the death of the **owner of the house**, that builder shall be **put to death**.

### § 230.—XXXV, 73-76.

¶ If the collapse causes the death of the **son of the owner** of the house, they shall **put to death the son of that builder**. <note>Babylonian law often applied the death penalty to the children of a perpetrator if the victim's own children were killed by the crime.</note>

### § 231.—XXXV, 77-81.

¶ If it causes the death of a **slave of the owner** of the house, he shall give **slave for slave** <gloss>b</gloss> to the owner of the house.

### § 225.

¶ If a **veterinary surgeon** <note>The text refers to a doctor of oxen or asses.</note> operates on an **ox** or a **donkey** for a severe wound and causes its death, he shall give to the owner of the animal **one-fourth** of its value.

### § 226.

¶ If a **barber** <term>gallabum</term> <note>The OCR identifies this professional as a 'brander,' but in Babylonian society, barbers were responsible for the hairstyles and marks that designated social status, including slavery.</note>, without the consent of the owner, shaves off or alters the **slave-mark** <term>abbutti</term> so that a slave cannot be recognized or sold, they shall **cut off the fingers** of that barber.

### § 227.

¶ If a man deceives a **barber** and causes him to mark a slave with the sign that he cannot be sold <note>Essentially helping a slave hide their status.</note>, they shall **put that man to death** and they shall cast him into his own house <note>This likely means he was to be buried under the ruins of his own home or executed at his doorstep.</note>. The barber shall **swear an oath** before the gods: "I did not mark him knowingly," and he shall go free.

### § 228.

¶ If a **builder** <term>itinnum</term> builds a house for a man and completes it, the owner shall give him **two shekels** <note>A shekel was approximately 8.3 grams of silver.</note> of silver per **SAR** <term>sar</term> <note>A Babylonian unit of area, roughly 36 square meters.</note> of the house as his wage.

### § 229.

¶ If a **builder** builds a house for a man but does not make its construction **firm**, and the house which he has built collapses and causes the **death of the owner** of the house, that builder shall be **put to death**.

### § 230.

¶ If the collapse causes the **death of a son** of the owner of the house, they shall **put to death a son of that builder**. <note>This is a literal application of the 'lex talionis' (law of retaliation) where the punishment exactly mirrors the crime, even affecting family members.</note>

### § 231.

¶ If it causes the **death of a slave** of the owner of the house, the builder shall give to the owner of the house a **slave of equal value**.

<summary>This section details the professional liabilities and standardized wages for barbers and builders in Babylon, applying the principle of life-for-a-life in cases of structural failure. It highlights the high stakes of professional work, where negligence could result in the execution of the professional or their kin.</summary>

<keywords>Code of Hammurabi, Babylonian law, builder liability, barber-surgeon, slave-marks, shekel, SAR, reciprocal justice, professional negligence</keywords>

<header>TRANSLATION</header>

### § 245.

¶ If a man hire an ox and cause its death through neglect or abuse, he shall restore an ox of equal value to the owner of the ox.

### § 246.

¶ If a man hire an ox and he break its foot or cut its ham-string <note>The original text refers to the neck tendon or ligament, though this translation suggests a leg tendon; in either case, it refers to a disabling injury to the animal's movement.</note>, he shall restore an ox of equal value to the owner of the ox.

### § 247.

¶ If a man hire an ox and destroy its eye, he shall pay silver to the owner of the ox to the extent of one-half its value.

### § 248.

¶ If a man hire an ox and break its horn or cut off its tail or injure the flesh through which the ring passes <note>This refers to the sensitive flesh of the muzzle where a lead ring was inserted to control the animal.</note>, he shall pay silver to the extent of one-fourth of its value.

### § 249.

¶ If a man hire an ox and a god strike it <note>A legal idiom for an "act of God," such as a lightning strike, a sudden plague, or a predator attack that the hirer could not have prevented.</note> and it die, the man who hired the ox shall take an oath before god and go free.

### § 250.

¶ If a bull, when passing through the street, gore a man and bring about his death, this case has no penalty <note>Because the event is considered a random accident in a public space, the owner is not held liable unless they knew the animal was dangerous.</note>.

### § 251.

¶ If a man’s bull have been wont to gore <note>Meaning the bull has a known history or habit of attacking.</note> and they have made known to him his habit of goring, and he have not protected his horns or have not tied him up, and that bull gore the son of a man and bring about his death, he shall pay one-half mana <term>mana</term> <note>A standard Babylonian unit of weight; one-half mana of silver was a significant fine, roughly 250 grams.</note> of silver.

**Vocabulary:** ox, hire, neglect, ham-string, silver, value, oath, bull, gore, penalty, mana of silver

### § 263.—XXXVIII, 37-43.

### § 264.—XXXVIII, 44-60.

¶ If a **shepherd** <note>original: "rê'um"</note> to whom cattle or sheep and goats have been given for pasturing has received his full wages as agreed and is satisfied, yet he allows the cattle or sheep to decrease in number, or causes the birth rate to decline, he shall make good the offspring and the produce according to the terms of his contract.

### § 265.—XXXVIII, 61-75.

¶ If a shepherd, to whom cattle or sheep and goats have been given for pasturing, acts dishonestly, or has **altered the brand** <note>original: "uštannit"; likely meaning he changed the ownership marks on the animals to hide a theft.</note>, or has sold them, they shall call him to account, and he shall restore to their owner cattle or sheep ten times the amount he has stolen.

¶ If a **visitation of god** <note>original: "lipit ilim"; literally "the touch of a god," referring to natural disasters, plagues, or lightning strikes.</note> occurs in a fold, or a **lion** kills, the shepherd shall declare himself innocent before god <note>This implies taking a sacred oath in the temple to prove he was not at fault.</note>, and the owner of the fold shall suffer the loss of the fold.

# EPILOGUE.

## TRANSLATION.

The righteous laws, which Hammurabi, the wise king, established and (by which) he gave the land stable support and pure government. Hammurabi, the perfect king, am I. I was not careless, nor was I neglectful of the **Black-Head people** <note>original: "ṣalmāt qaqqadim"; a traditional poetic term for the inhabitants of Mesopotamia, referring to all of humanity under the king's care.</note>, whose rule Bel <note>Also known as Enlil, the supreme god of the air and destiny.</note> presented and Marduk <note>The patron god of Babylon, elevated by Hammurabi to the head of the pantheon.</note> delivered to me. I provided them with a peaceful country. I opened up difficult barriers and lent them support. 

With the powerful weapon which Zamá-má <note>Also known as Zababa, a warrior god of the city of Kish.</note> and Nana <note>Referring here to Nanaya or Ishtar, the goddess of war and fertility.</note> entrusted to me, with the breadth of vision which Ea <note>Also known as Enki, the god of wisdom, crafts, and water.</note> allotted me, with the might which Marduk gave me, I expelled the enemy to the North and South; I made an end of their raids; I brought health to the land; I made the populace to rest in security; I permitted no one to molest them.

The great gods proclaimed me and I am the guardian governor, whose scepter is righteous and whose beneficent protection is spread over my city. In my bosom I carried the people of the land of **Sumer and Akkad** <note>The southern and central regions of Mesopotamia unified under Hammurabi’s rule.</note>; under my protection I brought their brethren into security; in my wisdom I restrained (hid) them; that the strong might not oppose the weak, and that they should give justice to the orphan and the widow, in Babylon, the city whose turrets Anu <note>The sky god and father of the gods.</note> and Bel raised; in **Esagila** <note>The great temple complex in Babylon dedicated to the god Marduk.</note>, the temple whose

<summary>In this epilogue, King Hammurabi declares his divine mandate and his success in bringing peace and security to Mesopotamia. He presents himself as a protective "shepherd" who uses his wisdom and military might to ensure justice for the vulnerable, specifically mentioning orphans and widows.</summary>

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI

...to judge the judgment of the land, to decide the decisions of the land, and to provide justice for the oppressed. My precious words I have written upon my monument <note>original: "narû"; refers to the stone stele or pillar on which the laws were inscribed.</note> and set up before my image <note>original: "ṣalmu"; a statue of the king that represents his physical and legal presence.</note> as the **King of Justice**. 

I am the king who is preeminent among kings. My words are choice; my wisdom has no rival. By the command of **Shamash** <note>The sun god, who was the supreme judge of heaven and earth and the source of all law.</note>, the great judge of heaven and earth, let my justice shine in the land. By the word of **Marduk**, my lord, let my monument find no one to damage it. In the **Esagila** <note>original: "E-sag-ila," meaning "House whose head is raised"; the main temple complex of Marduk in Babylon.</note>, which I love, let my name be remembered for good forever.

## COLUMN XLI.

Let it be remembered for all time: Let any oppressed man <note>original: "awīlum hablum"; a person who has suffered a legal or social wrong.</note> who has a legal case come before my image as the **King of Justice**. Let him read my inscribed monument. Let him give heed to my precious words. Let my monument explain the case to him; let him see his justice, and let his heart be set at ease. 

Let him say: "Hammurabi is indeed a lord who is like a biological father <note>original: "abi wālidi"; emphasizes the king's role as the life-giver and protector of his subjects.</note> to his people. He has carried out the word of Marduk, his lord, and has achieved victory for Marduk above and below. He has satisfied the heart of Marduk, his lord, and has provided well-being for the people forever and set the land in order."

Let him say this, and before Marduk, my lord, and **Zarpanitum** <note>The goddess and consort of Marduk, often associated with birth and mercy.</note>, my lady, let him pray for me with his whole heart. 

The **protective spirits** <note>original: "šēdum" and "lamassum"; winged guardian figures that protected entrances and individuals from evil.</note> and the gods who enter the Esagila, and the very bricks of the Esagila, let them daily speak well of me before Marduk, my lord, and Zarpanitum, my lady. 

In future days, for all time, let the king who arises in the land observe the words of justice which I have written on my monument. The judgment of the land which I have judged, the decisions of the land which I have decided...

He portrays himself as a father to his people and seeks the eternal favor of the gods Marduk and Zarpanitum.</summary>

# TRANSLATION

...foundations are as firm as heaven and earth. For the purpose of pronouncing judgments in the land, for the making of legal decisions for the country, and for the righting of wrongs, I have written my precious words upon my monument <note>original: "narû"; the stone stele.</note>, and I have established them in the presence of my statue as the **King of Justice**.

I am the king who is supreme among all city-kings. My words are precious; my wisdom has no equal. By the command of **Shamash** <note>The sun god, who served as the supreme judge of heaven and earth.</note>, the great judge of heaven and earth, may I cause justice to shine forth in the land. By the order of **Marduk** <note>The patron god of Babylon.</note>, my lord, may no one damage my statues, and may my name be remembered with favor in the **Esagila** <note>The main temple complex of Marduk in Babylon; the name means "House whose head is raised."</note> forever.

### COLUMN XLI

Let any oppressed man <note>original: "awīlum hablum"; a person who has suffered a legal or social wrong.</note> who has a legal case come before my statue as the **King of Justice**! Let him read the inscription on my monument! Let him pay close attention to my precious words! May my monument enlighten him regarding his case, and may he understand his rights! May his heart be set at ease! He will then exclaim:

> “Hammurabi is indeed a ruler who is like a true father to his people; he has shown reverence to the words of **Marduk**, his lord; he has achieved victory for Marduk in both the North and the South; he has brought joy to the heart of Marduk, his lord; he has established prosperity for the people for all time and provided a pure government for the land.”

Let him read the laws and pray with a full heart before **Marduk**, my lord, and **Zarpanit** <note>The goddess and consort of Marduk, often associated with birth and protection.</note>, my lady. May the protecting deities—the gods who enter the **Esagila**—daily look with favor upon his hopes and plans in the presence of Marduk and Zarpanit!

In the days that are yet to come, for all future time, let the king who rules the land observe the words of justice which I have written upon my monument! May he not alter the judgments of the land which I have pronounced, or the decisions of the country which I have rendered! May he not erase my...

May **Ninkarrak**, the daughter of **Anu** <note>original: *Annim*; the sky god and supreme ancestor of the deities.</note>, who speaks on my behalf in **E-kur** <note><term>E-kur</term>: The "Mountain House," the massive temple of the god Enlil in the city of Nippur, considered the religious center of the world.</note>, bring upon his body a grievous illness, an evil disease, a dangerous wound that cannot be healed, which the physician <note>original: *asu*; a medical specialist who treated ailments with herbs, ointments, and bandages.</note> cannot identify, which he cannot soothe with bandages, and which, like the bite of death, cannot be removed until it consumes his life! May he spend his days mourning the loss of his strength!

May the great gods of heaven and earth, the **Anunnaki** <note>The collective assembly of the highest-ranking deities in the Mesopotamian pantheon.</note> in their council, cast a terrible curse upon the temple walls, the very structure of this **E-babbarra** <note><term>E-babbarra</term>: The "Shining House" or "White House," the temple of the sun god Shamash, who was the divine patron of justice.</note>, as well as his descendants, his land, his army, his people, and his soldiers...

If a man has two wives in succession, the children shall inherit the dowries of their respective mothers; they shall share equally in their father’s estate, 167. <note>Under Babylonian law, a "dowry" (seriktu) was the property a woman brought into a marriage from her father's house, intended to support her and eventually her children.</note>

For incest the first time, 158.

However, they are not considered slaves, 171.
A wife has only a life interest in her dowry; it passes to her children after her death, 171.
A widow receives her dowry, 172.
If there was no marriage settlement, she must receive a portion of her husband’s estate equal to that of one child, 172. <note>A "marriage jointure" (nudunnu) was a gift given by the husband to the wife, distinct from the dowry she brought from her parents.</note>
A man's heirs cannot evict a widow from her home, 172.
A widow who remarries takes her dowry with her, but leaves any marriage settlement from her first husband to his children, 172.
If a widow remarries and has a second family, the two sets of children divide her dowry upon her death, 173.
If a widow remarries and has no second family, the children of her first husband inherit her dowry, 174.

**Witnesses** (in Babylonian simply “elders” <note>The Babylonian word for "witness" is the same as for "elder" (*shibu*), reflecting a society where the older, established members of the community acted as the guardians of truth and law.</note>):
1. witnesses, jury, elders of community, assessors of judgment <note>Assessors were individuals who sat alongside a judge to provide advice on local customs or technical matters.</note>.
   threats against them, or malicious reflections or insinuations, summarily punished, 3 <note>This refers to Law 3: If a witness provides false testimony in a capital case involving a life-or-death sentence, they face the death penalty.</note>.
   effort at bribery punished, 4.

**<term>KIŠŠATU</term>**, service: <note>original: "ki-iš-ša-tim," referring to the state of debt-slavery or service</note> *ki-iš-ša-tim*, **19**, 69; *ki-iš-ša-a-tim*, **19**, 59.

**<term>KIŠŠATU</term>**, everything, the universe: **1**, 12.

**<term>KAŠŪŠU</term>**, power, strength: <note>original: "ka-šu-ši-šu," often referring to a divine or overwhelming weapon/power</note> *ka-šu-ši-šu*, **44**, 29.

**<term>KATÂTU</term>**, <note>Verb Stem III, 2: a causative form</note>, to give reverence to: <note>original: "uš-ta-ak-ti-it," meaning "he has shown humility or reverence"</note> *uš-ta-ak-ti-it*, **41**, 27.

**<term>LÂ</term>**, negative, not.

**<term>LŪ</term>**, particle of emphasis: <note>Often used as "verily" or "indeed"</note>.

**<term>LŪ</term>**, precative particle: <note>A grammatical marker used to express a wish, such as "may he..."</note>.

**<term>MÂTU</term>** <note>original: "MÂTU"</note>, <note>Verb Stem I, 2: a completed action or perfect tense</note> *to die*: <note>original: "im-tu-ut"</note> *he has died*, **19**, 34, 42, **29**, 46, **33**, 28, **34**, 15, 32, 42, 52, **37**, 39.

<header>DISCOURSE 18.</header>

# ON BURIAL.

<margin>Genesis 23 and 25.</margin>
Many testimonies of Scripture prove that the duty of burial, which is performed for the deceased, is highly pleasing to God. For Abraham, in order to honorably bury his wife Sarah, purchased a field from the sons of Heth <note>original: "filiis Heth," referring to the Hittites mentioned in the Hebrew Bible</note>. Abraham himself, as well as Isaac and Jacob, were also buried in that same double cave <note>original: "spelunca duplici," traditionally identified as the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron</note>.

<margin>Tobit 1 and 2.</margin>
Tobit is greatly commended for this duty because he not only distributed his wealth to the needy, but would also rise from the table at night to gather and bury the bodies of murdered Jews. This service was so pleasing to God that He sent the Angel Raphael to accompany him and finally to restore his sight.

<margin>2 Samuel 2.</margin>
David also blessed the men of Jabesh-Gilead <note>A city east of the Jordan River whose inhabitants risked their lives to recover the bodies of the fallen King Saul and his sons from the Philistines</note> and gave them thanks because they had buried Saul and his son Jonathan.

<margin>Matthew 26, John 19.</margin>
Our Lord Jesus Christ himself praised that woman <note>Mary of Bethany</note> who had poured precious ointment on his head, saying that she had done this for his burial. And Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus are celebrated in the whole Church because they honorably buried his body after it was taken down from the cross.

<margin>Augustine, *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 3.</margin>
Hence Augustine says: *The bodies of the deceased must not be disregarded or neglected, especially those of the righteous and faithful, which the Holy Spirit used as tools and vessels for all good works.*

<margin>Socrates, Book 1, chapter 13.</margin>
And for this reason, even in the early Church, there was such care for burying the bodies of the Martyrs that many Christians exposed their lives to danger for this cause and were crowned with martyrdom.

<margin>Cyprian, Letter 2 to the Clergy.</margin>
Finally, Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage and influential Latin writer</note> writes that we ought to bury with the greatest diligence the bodies of those who die in prison for the faith, and to record the days of their deaths, so that their memory may be celebrated through annual sacrifices <note>original: "sacrificia," referring here to the commemorative Eucharist or "feast days" of the saints</note>.

<sig>Aa</sig>
<meta>catchword: lest</meta>

<summary>This page provides a theological defense of the sanctity of burial, citing Biblical figures like Abraham, Tobit, and David, as well as Church Fathers like Augustine and Cyprian, to argue that burying the dead is a duty pleasing to God.</summary>

<language>Latin</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>686</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER II.</header>

# ON THE KINDS AND DIFFERENCES OF SACRIFICE.

<margin>Division of sacrifice based on its purpose.</margin>
First, sacrifice in general is divided according to the diversity of its purpose: for it is either offered to God to honor him and acknowledge him as the supreme Lord, in which case it is called a **burnt offering** <note>original: "holocauston" or "holocautomata", terms derived from the Greek meaning "wholly burnt," where the entire offering was consumed by fire</note>; or it is offered to obtain the forgiveness of sins, called a **propitiatory sacrifice**, or a **sin offering**; or it is offered to give thanks for benefits received, or to obtain new benefits, and is called a **eucharistic sacrifice** <note>In this historical context, "eucharistic" refers generally to "thanksgiving," from the Greek "eucharistia"</note>, or a **peace offering**. The Church Fathers frequently pass down this division, and it is found in *Exodus 29*, *Leviticus 8*, and often elsewhere.

<margin>Based on the material.</margin>
Second, the division of sacrifices must be sought from their material: for it either consists of a living thing, and then it is called a **victim** or **host**; or it consists of an inanimate thing, and is called a **libation** or an **offering**. This is the common interpretation among commentators on *Leviticus 1*.

<margin>Based on the rite.</margin>
Third, the division is to be sought from the rite and manner of sacrificing: for there were some sacrifices in which the whole animal was burned, and these were called **burnt offerings**; others in which one part was burned, while another part went to the use of the priests or the offerers, and these were called **sin offerings** or **peace offerings**.

<margin>Bloody and unbloody sacrifice.</margin>
Fourth, sacrifice is divided into **bloody** and **unbloody**. A bloody sacrifice is one in which there is an effusion of blood through the killing of a victim; such was the sacrifice of Christ on the cross, concerning which *Isaiah 53:10* says: *If he makes his soul an offering for sin*. All the sacrifices of the Old Law, in which livestock were killed, were **bloody**. An unbloody sacrifice is one in which no shedding of blood occurs, such as the sacrifice of Melchisedech <note>A priest-king from the Book of Genesis who offered bread and wine instead of animals</note> in bread and wine (*Genesis 14*), and the Sacrifice of the Mass, which is the representation and application of Christ's bloody sacrifice.

<margin>Legal and Evangelical sacrifice.</margin>
Fifth, it is divided into **legal** and **Evangelical**. The legal sacrifices were all those instituted by Moses, which were shadows and figures of things to come. The Evangelical sacrifice is that single sacrifice of Christ, performed partly on the Cross and continued partly in the Mass.

<margin>External and internal sacrifices.</margin>
Sixth, it is divided into **external** and **internal**. An external sacrifice is that outward act by which some sensible thing is offered to God. An internal sacrifice is the inward act of the mind and heart, by which a person offers themselves to God through faith, hope, and charity, or through penance, according to *Psalm 50*: *A broken spirit is a sacrifice to God*.

<margin>Symbolic and true.</margin>
Seventh, sacrifice is divided into **symbolic** and **true** or **real**. It is called symbolic when it is not in itself and properly a sacrifice, but is only called such metaphorically: such as the sacrifice of praise, prayer, penance, etc., which we shall discuss below. A true and real sacrifice is that which possesses all the conditions required for a true sacrifice, which were discussed in the preceding chapter.

<margin>Sacrifices of Christ and the faithful.</margin>
Eighth, finally, sacrifices can be divided into the **Sacrifice of Christ** and the **Sacrifice of the faithful**. The Sacrifice of Christ is that which Christ himself offered on the Cross, and daily offers on the Altar through the hands of priests. The sacrifice of the faithful is that which all Christians offer to God when they dedicate and consecrate themselves to God along with Christ, according to *Romans 12*: *Offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God*. But this division is not strictly proper, since the sacrifice of the faithful is such only by participation and metaphor, as we shall soon say. That which remains to be discussed in this section concerns only sacrifice properly so called, specifically that which existed in the law of nature and that which existed in the written law, which we will deal with in the following chapters.

The first question asked here is whether, under the law of nature, any sacrifice

# PART TWO.

->PART TWO<-

<margin>How the twenty-four elders sit.</margin>
The manner in which the twenty-four elders sit is declared: *Around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, and on their heads were crowns of gold.* <note>original: "Circumquaque thronum... coronæ aureæ." This is a translation of Revelation 4:4.</note>

<margin>What does the number 24 signify?</margin>
By these twenty-four elders are denoted all the saints, of both the Old and the New Testament, who reign in heaven: as is first stated by all the glosses <note>marginal or interlinear commentaries used by medieval scholars</note> and expositors, especially *St. Thomas Aquinas in the Secunda Secundæ, Question 2, Article 7, Reply to the 3rd objection; and in Book 1 of the Summa contra Gentiles, Chapter 101.* And they are called twenty-four, partly because of the twelve Patriarchs, from whom the people of Israel and consequently the entire Synagogue <note>here referring to the assembly of the Old Covenant</note> arose; and partly because of the twelve Apostles, who are the foundations of the Church and through whom the faith of Christ was spread. Thus, the holiness of the Old and New Testaments completes this number.

<margin>Why do they sit near the throne?</margin>
These elders sit on thrones around the Throne of God: partly to indicate their state of rest, as they find repose from their labors; and partly to denote their judicial power, which they shall have on the Day of Judgment, according to the scripture: *You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* <note>original: "Sedebitis & vos... iudicantes duodecim tribus Iſraël." From Matthew 19:28.</note> Finally, it is to show their friendship and familiarity with God, and the divine enjoyment they have upon their thrones: for to sit next to a King is a sign of honor and intimacy.

<margin>Why are they called elders?</margin>
They are called *elders*, however, not because of their age: for on the day of resurrection, everyone will be of a youthful and perfect age, similar to the age of Christ when He underwent death <note>traditionally held to be 33 years old</note>, as *St. Augustine teaches in Book 22 of The City of God, chapters 15 and 16; St. Thomas in the 4th book of the Sentences, distinction 44;* and the common opinion of all theologians. Rather, they are called elders because of their gravity, wisdom, and the maturity of their lives; and also to show the antiquity and firmness of the faith which they held.

<margin>Why are they clothed in white garments?</margin>
They are said to be clothed in *white garments*: partly because of the brilliance and purity of their souls, which have no stain; and partly because of the glory of their bodies, which after the resurrection will be most radiant and white within them. For whiteness is a symbol of glory and blessedness: hence Christ, in His Transfiguration, appeared in white garments,

<column-break/>

as it is also said later regarding the blessed: *They shall walk with me in white, for they are worthy.* <note>original: "Ambulabunt mecum in albis..." From Revelation 3:4.</note>

<margin>Why do they have golden crowns?</margin>
They also have *on their heads golden crowns*: by which their royal dignity is designated: *For You have made us a kingdom and priests for our God.* <note>original: "Feciſti enim nos Deo noſtro regnum, & ſacerdotes." From Revelation 5:10.</note> Likewise, the crown is the reward of the victory by which they overcame the world, the flesh, and the devil. They are golden to denote the preciousness and eternity of their glory: just as gold is the most precious metal and is the least subject to corruption.

<margin>What do the four living creatures signify?</margin>
Next, the four living creatures are described, which were in the midst of the throne and around the throne: *And in the midst of the throne, and around the throne, were four living creatures full of eyes before and behind. And the first creature was like a lion, and the second creature like a calf, and the third creature had a face like a man, and the fourth creature was like a flying eagle. And the four living creatures each had six wings: and they were full of eyes within and around.* <note>original: "Et in medio ſedis... plena ſunt oculis." This is a translation of Revelation 4:6-8.</note>

<margin>Various interpretations.</margin>
Regarding the meaning of these four living creatures, there are many opinions among the doctors. Some understand these four creatures to be the four Evangelists: as *St. Jerome in the preface to Matthew; St. Gregory in Book 4 on Ezekiel; St. Ambrose in the preface to Luke; Bede, and others throughout.* For Matthew is compared to the man, because he begins with the human genealogy of Christ; Mark to the lion, because he begins with the voice of one crying in the wilderness, which suits a lion; Luke to the calf <note>or ox</note>, because he begins with the priesthood of Zechariah, whose duty it was to sacrifice calves; and John to the eagle, because he flew higher than the others to contemplate the divinity of the Word. Some understand these creatures to be the principal mysteries of our Redemption performed in Christ: who was a *Man* in being born, a *Calf* in dying, a *Lion* in rising, and an *Eagle* in ascending: as *St. Gregory* says in the place cited. Some understand them to be the four principal virtues that ought to be in apostolic men and all prelates of the Church: namely, fortitude through the lion, humility and patience through the calf, prudence through the man, and the contemplation of divine things through the eagle. But the more common and more literal explanation is that by these four creatures are understood the four Cherubim or Seraphim, who are the most excellent angels, standing <meta>The text continues with "before" (assistentur) on the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page provides a theological commentary on the Book of Revelation, specifically identifying the twenty-four elders as representatives of the Old and New Testaments and interpreting the symbolism of the four living creatures.</summary>
<keywords>Apocalypse, Twenty-Four Elders, Four Living Creatures, Evangelists, Thomas Aquinas, St. Augustine, Heavenly Throne, Biblical Symbolism</keywords>

## COLUMN VIII.

---

<margin>5</margin>
<image-desc>The lower section of the second column, containing the first eight lines of a new section of text identified as Column VIII, written in cuneiform script.</image-desc>

# PART TWO.

->PART TWO<-

<margin>How the twenty-four elders sit.</margin>
The manner in which the twenty-four elders sit is declared: *Around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, and on their heads were crowns of gold.* <note>original Latin: "Circumquaque thronum... coronæ aureæ." This is a translation of Revelation 4:4.</note>

<margin>What does the number 24 signify?</margin>
By these twenty-four elders are denoted all the saints, of both the Old and the New Testament, who reign in heaven: as is first stated by all the glosses <note>marginal or interlinear commentaries used by medieval scholars</note> and expositors, especially *St. Thomas Aquinas in the Second Part of the Second Part <note>original: "Secunda Secundæ"</note>, Question 2, Article 7, Reply to the 3rd objection; and in Book 1 of the Summary against the Gentiles <note>original: "Summa contra Gentiles"</note>, Chapter 101.* And they are called twenty-four, partly because of the twelve Patriarchs, from whom the people of Israel and consequently the entire Synagogue <note>here referring to the assembly of the Old Covenant</note> arose; and partly because of the twelve Apostles, who are the foundations of the Church and through whom the faith of Christ was spread. Thus, the holiness of the Old and New Testaments completes this number.

<margin>Why do they sit near the throne?</margin>
These elders sit on thrones around the Throne of God: partly to indicate their state of rest, as they find repose from their labors; and partly to denote their judicial power, which they shall have on the Day of Judgment, according to the scripture: *You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* <note>original Latin: "sedebitis et vos super sedes duodecim, iudicantes duodecim tribus Israel." A reference to Matthew 19:28.</note>

<summary>This page contains a medieval theological commentary on the twenty-four elders from the Book of Revelation, explaining their number as a union of the twelve Patriarchs and twelve Apostles. The text interprets their seated position around God's throne as a symbol of both eternal rest and their future role in divine judgment.</summary>
<keywords>Book of Revelation, twenty-four elders, Thomas Aquinas, twelve Patriarchs, twelve Apostles, heavenly court, symbolism of numbers, Day of Judgment</keywords>

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI PLATE XII

...[if a man takes a wife and] <margin>6</margin> a chronic illness <note>original Akkadian: "la'bu," likely referring to a persistent, debilitating skin disease or fever</note> seizes her, and he determines <margin>10</margin> to marry another woman, he may marry. His wife whom the illness has seized he shall not divorce; <margin>15</margin> she shall dwell in the house they have built together, and he shall continue to support her as long as she lives.

**Law 149:** If that woman <margin>20</margin> does not wish to dwell in her husband’s house, he shall make good to her the dowry <note>original: "seriqtu," the assets brought by the bride from her father's house</note> which she brought from the house of her father, and <margin>25</margin> she may depart.

<image-desc>The right column continues the cuneiform inscription from line 26 through line 52. The text is organized into horizontal registers with signs varying in complexity from simple single wedges to complex clusters.</image-desc>

**Law 150:** If a man <margin>26</margin> deeds to his wife a field, a garden, a house, or goods, and leaves a sealed deed for her, after her husband has gone to his fate <note>a standard Babylonian euphemism for death</note>, <margin>30</margin> her children shall not press a claim against her. The mother may give her legacy to the child whom she loves, but she is not required <margin>35</margin> to give it to an outsider <note>literally "to a brother," implying the husband's kin or perhaps an ungrateful child</note>.

**Law 151:** If a woman who dwells in a man's house binds her husband by a contract <margin>40</margin> that no creditor of her husband shall seize her, and he provides a written deed; if that man had a debt before he took that woman, his creditors <margin>45</margin> may not seize his wife. And if that woman had a debt before she entered the man's house, her creditors may not seize her husband.

**Law 152:** If, after that woman has entered the man's house, <margin>50</margin> a debt is incurred by them, both of them shall satisfy the merchant.

**Law 153:** If a woman, because of another man, causes the death of her husband, they shall impale <margin>52</margin> that woman on a stake.

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI PLATE XVII

<margin>Col. XI.</margin>

**Law 162:** ...If a man takes a wife and she bears him children, and that woman then goes to her fate <note>original: "ana šīmtim ittalak"; a common euphemism for death</note>, her father shall have no claim to her dowry <term>dowry: (šeriktum) property or money brought by the bride from her father's house into the new household to support her and her children</term>. <margin>20</margin>

**Law 163:** If a man takes a wife and she does not bear him children, and that woman then goes to her fate, if the bride-price <note>original: "terḥatum"</note> which that man brought to the house of his father-in-law has been returned to him, her father shall have no claim to her dowry.

<margin>25</margin>

**Law 164:** If his father-in-law has not returned the bride-price to him, the husband shall deduct the value of the bride-price from her dowry and return the remainder of her dowry to her father’s house.

<margin>30</margin>

**Law 165:** If a man grants a field, an orchard, or a house to his favorite heir <note>literally "the son who is first in his eyes"</note> and provides a sealed document for him, then when the father goes to his fate, 

<margin>35</margin>

and the brothers divide the estate, the favorite son shall first take the gift his father gave him, and beyond that, they shall all divide the property of the paternal estate equally.

<column-break/>

**Law 166:** If a man takes wives for his older sons, but does not take a wife for his youngest son, and then the father goes to his fate—

<margin>40</margin>

when the brothers divide the estate, they shall set aside from the property of the paternal estate the money for a bride-price <note>original: "terḥatum"</note> for their younger brother who has not yet taken a wife, in addition to his equal share, 

<margin>45</margin>

and they shall enable him to take a wife.

**Law 167:** If a man takes a wife and she bears him children, and that woman goes to her fate, and after her he takes another wife 

<margin>50</margin>

who also bears him children—if the father then goes to his fate, the children shall not divide the estate based on the mothers' standing. 

<margin>55</margin>

The children shall take the dowries of their respective mothers and then they shall divide the property of their father’s estate equally among all the brothers.

<margin>60</margin>

If a man hires a field-laborer, he shall pay him eight *gur* <note>A *gur* was a large Babylonian unit of volume, approximately 300 liters or 8.5 bushels</note> of grain per year.

<margin>45</margin>
If a man hires a herdsman, he shall pay him six *gur* of grain per year.

<margin>50</margin>
If a man hires an ox for threshing <note>The process of loosening the edible part of grain from the husks</note>, its hire is twenty *qa* <note>A *qa* was approximately 0.8 to 1 liter</note> of grain.

<margin>55</margin>
If an ass is hired for threshing, its hire is ten *qa* of grain. If a young animal is hired for threshing, its hire is one *qa* of grain.

<image-desc>Block of Akkadian cuneiform text representing lines 38 through 59 of Column XII of the Code of Hammurabi. The characters are inscribed in a monumental lapidary style, with horizontal ruled lines separating each row of text.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

<margin>60</margin>
If a man hires oxen, a wagon, and its driver, he shall pay one hundred and eighty *qa* of grain per day.

<margin>65</margin>
If a man hires a wagon alone, he shall pay forty *qa* of grain per day.

## COLUMN XIII.

<margin>5</margin>
If a man hires a day-laborer, from the beginning of the year <note>The Babylonian New Year began in the spring, around the vernal equinox</note> until the fifth month, he shall pay six *grains* <note>original: "še"; here used as a tiny unit of weight for silver, roughly 0.046 grams</note> of silver per day.

<margin>10</margin>
From the sixth month until the end of the year, he shall pay five *grains* of silver per day.

<image-desc>Initial section of Column XIII of the Code of Hammurabi in Akkadian cuneiform script, containing lines 1 through 13. The text is organized similarly into horizontal registers.</image-desc>

<term>Gur: A Babylonian dry measure used primarily for large quantities of grain, essential for calculating annual salaries in an agrarian economy.</term>

<term>Qa: A smaller unit of capacity; sixty qa typically made up one *pi*, and five *pi* made up one *gur*.</term>

<term>Grain (Weight): In a pre-coinage economy, silver was weighed; a "grain" was the smallest unit, representing 1/180th of a shekel.</term>

<summary>This page outlines the legally mandated wages for agricultural workers and the fixed rental prices for threshing animals and transport wagons. It demonstrates the Babylonian state's role in regulating the economy by setting price floors and ceilings for labor and equipment hire.</summary>

<margin>1</margin> If a man seizes an ox as <term>distraint</term> <note>original: "nepûm"; the legal seizure of property to satisfy a debt.</note>, he shall pay one-third of a <term>mina</term> of silver. <note>This law protected a farmer's livelihood; even if a farmer owed money, the creditor could not seize the ox needed for plowing without facing a heavy fine.</note>

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI
## PLATE XXXVI

### COLUMN XXII (THE EPILOGUE)

<margin>Col. XXII</margin>

<margin>30</margin> By the command of Shamash, the great judge of heaven and earth, may my justice shine in the land. By the word of Marduk, my lord, may no one mar my monument. <note>Shamash was the sun god and the patron of justice; Marduk was the patron deity of Babylon. Hammurabi attributes the permanence of his laws to their divine protection.</note> In <term>Esagila</term> <note>original: "E-sag-ila"; the great temple complex in Babylon dedicated to Marduk.</note> which I love, may my name be remembered for good forever.

<margin>35</margin> The king who provides for the people, the king of power, am I. Through the wisdom that Marduk gave me and the might that <term>Enlil</term> <note>One of the supreme deities of the Mesopotamian pantheon, associated with kingship and the air.</note> bestowed upon me, 

<margin>40</margin> I uprooted the enemy above and below; I ended strife; I brought well-being to the land. I caused the people of the settlements to rest in security; I did not allow anyone to terrorize them.

<margin>45</margin> The great gods called me, and I am the shepherd who brings peace, whose staff is straight. <note>The "straight staff" is a metaphor for both the literal shepherd’s tool and the king’s scepter of honest, upright rule.</note> My protective shadow is spread over my city.

<column-break/>

<margin>50</margin> In my bosom, I carried the people of the land of Sumer and Akkad. <note>original: "Šumerim u Akkadîm"; referring to the combined regions of Southern and Central Mesopotamia that Hammurabi unified.</note> Under my protection, they prospered in peace; in my wisdom, I sheltered them.

<margin>55</margin> So that the strong might not oppress the weak, and to provide justice for the orphan and the widow, I have inscribed my precious words upon my monument and set it up in Babylon before my image as the "King of Justice."

<margin>60</margin> Let any oppressed man who has a legal suit come before my image as the King of Justice; let him read the inscription on my monument and give heed to my weighty words. <note>This suggests the stela was placed in a public area—likely the temple courtyard—where citizens were encouraged to consult the law to understand their rights.</note>

<margin>65</margin> May my monument reveal the law to him; may he understand his case, and may his heart be set at ease, 

<margin>70</margin> so that he may say: "Hammurabi is indeed a ruler who is like a biological father to his people. He has submitted himself to the word of Marduk, his lord, and has achieved victory for Marduk above and below."

<summary>In this portion of the epilogue, Hammurabi transitions from law-giving to self-glorification, presenting himself as a divinely appointed shepherd and father to his people. He explicitly states that the purpose of the stela is to provide a public, readable record of justice for the oppressed.</summary>
<keywords>Epilogue, Shamash, Marduk, Esagila, Sumer and Akkad, King of Justice, Oppressed, Monument Preservation, Shepherding Metaphor</keywords>

<margin>51</margin> Under my protection, I sheltered them in peace; in my wisdom, I shielded them.

<margin>60</margin> So that the strong might not oppress the weak, and to provide justice for the orphan and the widow, <note>Protecting widows and orphans was a standard of the "just king" in Mesopotamian rhetoric, signifying a leader who looks after those without a male protector.</note> in Babylon—the city whose foundations <term>Anu</term> <note>The sky god and supreme deity of the pantheon.</note> and Enlil have made firm—in <term>Esagila</term>, the temple whose foundations are as stable as the heavens and the earth, 

<margin>70</margin> for the judgment of the land to be decided, for the legal decisions of the land to be rendered, and for the oppressed to be righted, I have written my precious words upon my monument.

<margin>75</margin> I have set it up before my own image as the king of justice.

<margin>80</margin> I am the king who is preeminent among kings. My words are choice; my power has no rival.

# Chapter Three. <note>original: "Caput tertium"</note>
## On the Natural State.

**1.** <margin>1. The state of men outside of civil society, which is rightly called the natural state, is nothing other than War, and indeed a war of all against all.</margin> The state of men outside of civil society (which state one may naturally name) is none other than a War of all against all; the cause of this war is this: that Nature has given to everyone a right to all things. In the natural state, however, the appetites of men who desire the same thing generally drive them to war.

**2.** <margin>2. The cause of this war is that all people simultaneously desire the same thing and have a right to all things.</margin> <margin>3. The appetites of men are generally directed toward the same thing, from which war arises.</margin> But if the appetites of two people are directed toward the same thing, which cannot be possessed or divided by both at once, it is necessary that one must yield or the right must be fought for. In the natural state, however, where there is no Judge but the sword, that struggle is inevitable.

**3.** <margin>4. In the natural state, everyone has a right to all things.</margin> Nature has given to everyone a right to all things. That is, in a purely natural state, or before men had bound themselves to one another by any agreements, everyone was permitted to do whatever and to whomever they pleased; and to possess, use, and enjoy all things that they wanted and were able to. For since everything a person does is said to be done by right reason if they strive to do it for their own preservation: and since in the natural state everyone is their own judge of what is necessary for their own preservation; it follows from this that everything a person does is done by the right of nature. And from this comes that axiom: *Nature has given all things to everyone.* <note>original: "Naturam dedisse omnia omnibus"</note>

**4.** <margin>5. From this right, no benefit arises, but rather perpetual war.</margin> From this right to all things, which everyone possesses, no benefit arises. For even if anyone can say of any thing, *this is mine*; <note>original: "hoc meum est"</note> yet they cannot enjoy it because of their neighbor, who with similar right and equal force contends that the same thing is his own. From here, therefore, arise perpetual suspicions and traps; from here, war, in which force and deceit are the cardinal virtues. In this war, nothing is unjust. For where there is no common power, there is no law: where there is no law, there is no injustice. Finally, in this state there is no property, no ownership, no distinct *mine* or *thine* <note>original: "meum aut tuum"</note>; but only that belongs to each person which they can seize, and for as long as they can keep it. And this is the most miserable condition, in which the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, and short. <note>original: "solitaria, inops, bruta, et brevis"</note>

**5.** <margin>6. The natural state is not a state of liberty, but of misery and slavery.</margin> Nor should this state be called a state of liberty, but rather one of misery and slavery. For, although in that state everyone is free from every human law, they are nonetheless under the empire of all their passions, and under the perpetual fear of a violent death. True liberty is not being able to be forced to that which is evil; which is found only in the <term>Civitas</term> <note>The "Civitas" refers to the organized State or Commonwealth, where a central authority maintains order.</note>.

**6.** <margin>7. How one must exit from this state.</margin> Since, therefore, this state is so miserable, reason dictates to everyone that they should strive to exit from it. Now, the means by which one exits this state are the *Laws of Nature*, and *Covenants* or *Agreements*, by which men transfer their right to all things to others, in order to obtain peace. These things, however, cannot be done in any other way than through the institution of a State [Commonwealth], in which a supreme power is established, which keeps everyone in their duty through the fear of punishment. Without this fear, agreements and laws are empty instruments...

<summary>This page outlines Thomas Hobbes's famous philosophical concept of the "State of Nature," arguing that without a central government, human life is a constant "war of all against all" where no one is safe and no property is secure.</summary>
<keywords>State of Nature, Thomas Hobbes, War of all against all, Natural Right, Social Contract, Sovereignty, Civil Society, Liberty vs. Security</keywords>
