# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI PLATE XLV
## Epilogue: Column XXVII

<margin>Col. XXVII.</margin>

If that man <note>Referring to any future ruler or person of authority</note> does not pay attention to my words which I have inscribed upon my monument; if he disregards my curses and does not fear the curses of the gods; if he abolishes the law which I have given, distorts my words, or alters my carvings;

<margin>10</margin>
or if, to escape these curses, he erases my inscribed name and writes his own name <note>Original: "shumi shatram upasshish-ma" — the act of "name-erasing" was considered a spiritual execution in the ancient Near East, as a person's name was tied to their eternal legacy</note>; or if he instructs another to do so:

<margin>15</margin>
whether that man be a king, a lord, a governor <note>Original: "shakkanakkum" — a high-ranking military or provincial official</note>, or any person of renown,

<margin>20</margin>
may the great Anu, the father of the gods, who has decreed my reign, strip away from him the splendor of royalty;

<margin>25</margin>
may he break his scepter and curse his destiny.

<column-break/>

<margin>30</margin>
May Anu <note>The sky god and supreme authority of the Mesopotamian pantheon</note> decree for him a reign of sighing, days that are few in number, and years of famine.

<margin>35</margin>
May he decree for him darkness without light, and a death that is visible to all eyes.

<margin>40</margin>
May Enlil <note>The god of the air and the "Lord of Lands" who determines the fates of nations</note>, the lord who determines destinies, whose command cannot be altered, and who has made my dominion great,

<margin>45</margin>
incite against him in his own city a rebellion that his hand cannot suppress. May he send a wind of destruction to blow upon his dwelling.

<margin>50</margin>
May he decree for him a reign of misery, days of hardship, and years of want.

<meta>Translator Note: There is a significant thematic and linguistic shift from the previous page. While the previous section concluded the Epilogue of the Code of Hammurabi (Old Babylonian cuneiform), this page transitions into a Latin legal treatise, likely from the Early Modern period, discussing the principles of Roman law and the definitions of judicial authority.</meta>

## V.
<margin>What jurisdiction is and what its types are</margin>
To decide between right and wrong, and to take knowledge of the controversies of citizens, and to pronounce judgment, and to judge, is called jurisdiction <note>original: "iurisdictio"</note>. And it is twofold: one part is civil, the other is criminal. Civil <note>original: "civilis"</note> is that by which the private legal actions, business matters, and damages among the citizens themselves are examined. Criminal <note>original: "criminalis"</note>, however, is that by which inquiry is made into crimes and misdeeds for the purpose of inflicting punishment.

## VI.
<margin>What *imperium* is</margin>
*Imperium* <term>Imperium: A Latin term referring to the supreme administrative and executive power of the state, particularly the right to command and enforce obedience.</term> is public power and the right of commanding <note>original: "ius iussendi"</note>, which is granted to a magistrate in the name of the State <note>original: "Reipublicae"</note>, and to whose command all citizens are bound to obey. To judges and praetors <note>high-ranking Roman judicial officers responsible for the administration of justice</note>, indeed, is granted the right of commanding those who are subject to their jurisdiction. Furthermore, this right of commanding belongs not so much to the specific persons as to the office of the magistrate <note>original: "magistratus"</note>: therefore, it ceases once the magistrate has stepped down from office.

<note>Vocabulary used in this section: jurisdiction (iurisdictio), civil (civilis), criminal (criminalis), command (imperium), public power (potestas publica), magistrate (magistratus), right of commanding (ius iussendi).</note>

<summary>This page defines the fundamental legal concepts of jurisdiction and command (imperium), distinguishing between civil and criminal law and explaining that authority resides in the office of the magistrate rather than the individual person.</summary>
<keywords>jurisdiction, civil law, criminal law, imperium, magistracy, Roman law, legal authority</keywords>

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI PLATE LI

<margin>Col. XXX.</margin>

If that man does not heed my words which I have written on my stele <note>a tall stone monument used for inscriptions</note>, and if he disregards my curses and does not fear the curses of the gods, but instead abolishes the law which I have given, or distorts my words, or alters my statues, or even effaces my name in order to write his own name—or if, out of fear of these curses, he appoints someone else to do so—

<margin>15</margin>

Whether he be a king, or a lord, or a governor, or any person of whatever name, may the great **Anu**, the father of the gods, who has named my reign, take from him the splendor of royalty; may he break his scepter <note>original: "haitum"</note> and curse his destiny.

<margin>20</margin>

May **Enlil**, the lord who determines fates, whose command cannot be altered, and who has made my kingdom great, stir up against him a rebellion in his own house that his hand cannot suppress.

<margin>25</margin>

May he cause a wind of destruction to blow against his reign; may he decree as his fate a reign of sighing, short days, and years of hunger.

<margin>30</margin>

May he decree the ruin of his city and the dispersion of his people <note>original: "nišū"</note>.

<column-break/>

May **Enlil**, by his powerful word, pronounce a curse that cannot be turned aside, and may it quickly overtake him.

<margin>35</margin>

May **Nintu**, the sublime mistress of the lands, the mother who gave me birth, deny him an heir; may she not grant him a son among his people.

<margin>40</margin>

May **Enki**, the great prince, whose decrees take precedence, the leader of the gods, who knows all things, who prolongs the days of my life, take away his wisdom and his cleverness.

<margin>45</margin>

May he lead him into forgetfulness, and may he dam up his rivers at their sources <note>an ancient Mesopotamian metaphor for cutting off the lifeblood and resources of a kingdom</note>.

<margin>50</margin>

May he prevent the growth of grain <note>original: "ašnan"</note> in his land, so that the people may not have the life-giving bread.

<margin>55</margin>

May **Shamash**, the great judge of heaven and earth, who guides all living creatures, the lord of confidence, shatter his kingdom.

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI PLATE LIII

<margin>Col. XXXI.</margin>

May **Adad** <note>The Mesopotamian god of storms, thunder, and rain, responsible for both life-giving water and destructive floods</note>, the lord of abundance, the irrigator of heaven and earth, my helper, withhold from him the rain from heaven and the water-floods from the springs.

<margin>30</margin>

<margin>40</margin>

<margin>45</margin>

<margin>50</margin>

### At a General Assembly of the Governor and Company of the English Colony
### of Connecticut in New England in America held at Hartford on the
### second Thursday of May, being the 11th day of the said month, in the year 1749.

Regarding the petition of John Hart of Farmington and others—who are residents and <term>Proprietors</term> <note>Landowners who held legal title to shared or individual lands within a township</note> of the lands in the first <term>Society</term> <note>In colonial Connecticut, a "Society" was an ecclesiastical district or parish. These were often the primary units of local government, responsible for the church, schools, and local taxes</note> in Farmington, as well as landowners in the tenth Society in Farmington (called Northington <note>Now the town of Avon, Connecticut</note>) and the ninth Society in Farmington (called New-Cambridge <note>Now the city of Bristol, Connecticut</note>)—stating to this Assembly that the boundaries of these Societies have never been fully and accurately defined or settled. They report that because of this, many inconveniences have occurred or may arise. They ask this Assembly to appoint a committee to view, examine, and determine the boundaries and lines of these three Societies and report back to the Assembly this coming October.

It is resolved by this Assembly that Colonel John Chester, Captain Jonathan Hills, and Mr. Joseph Wells are hereby appointed as a committee to inspect and examine the lines and boundaries of the first, ninth, and tenth Societies in Farmington. They are to notify all involved parties to attend the proceedings. They must report their findings and their formal opinion to this Assembly in October. Furthermore, John Hart and the other petitioners are responsible for giving the committees of each Society ten days' notice before the scheduled meeting of the appointed committee.

->A true Copy of the Record,<-
->Examined by George Wyllys, Secretary<-

# CHAPTER XIV. CONCERNING SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST. <note>original: "CAP. XIV. DE S. IOANNE BAPTISTA."</note>

<margin>
Saint John the Baptist.
His birth and parents.
</margin>
I. **JOHN** (whose name is interpreted as *the grace of God* <note>original: "Dei gratia"</note>) was born in the year of the world 3996, in the first year before the beginning of the *common Christian era*, on the 24th day of June, a Saturday. He was the son of *Zacharias* the Priest and *Elizabeth*, a kinswoman of the Blessed Virgin Mary. He was conceived in the second year before the *common era*, on the 24th day of September, the fifth day of the week <note>Thursday</note>, which was the Day of Expiation <note>Yom Kippur</note>. On that day, while *Zacharias* was performing his duties in the sanctuary, he received the promise concerning a son from an Angel. *Luke 1:5.*

<margin>
Isaiah 40:3.
Malachi 3:1.
and 4:5.
</margin>
II. This is the one of whom *Isaiah* foretold: *The voice of one crying in the wilderness, etc. chapter 40:3.* And *Malachi: Behold, I send my Angel, who shall prepare the way before my face. chapter 3:1.* Likewise: *Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. chapter 4:5.* That this prophecy was to be understood not as *Elijah the Tishbite*, but as *John the Baptist*, Christ himself testified in plain words in *Matthew 11:14 and 17:10*, as did the Angel in *Luke 1:17.*

<margin>
The precursor of Christ.
</margin>
III. Moreover, he was the precursor <note>one who runs before; a herald</note> of Christ in three ways: 1. *By his preaching:* for he preached penance and the arrival of the *Messiah* who was already present. *Matthew 3:1; Luke 3:2; John 1:19.* 2. *By his baptism:* by which he prepared penitent men for the kingdom of the *Messiah*. *Luke 3:3.* 3. *By the pointing of his finger:* saying, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." <note>original: "ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi"</note> *John 1:29.*

<margin>
He performed no miracles.
</margin>
IV. He himself performed no miracles, *John 10:41.* Nevertheless, he was a *Prophet*, and more than a *Prophet*. *Matthew 11:9.* And among those born of women, none has arisen greater than he, as stated in the same place, *verse 11.*

<margin>
Food and clothing.
</margin>
V. He was, however, most austere in his dress and diet. For he was clothed in camel's hair, with a leathern belt around his loins; and his food was locusts and wild honey. *Matthew 3:4.*

<margin>
Beheaded.
</margin>
VI. He was cast into chains by *Herod Antipas* (whom he had openly rebuked because he had joined himself in marriage to *Herodias*, the wife of his brother *Philip*) and was finally beheaded in prison. *Matthew 14:3.*

<margin>
The Feast of Saint John.
</margin>
VII. His memory (both of his birth and his beheading) is celebrated in the Church. His *Nativity* is observed on the 24th day of June, and his *Beheading* on the 29th day of August—the same day on which his father *Zacharias* was also formerly honored.

<summary>This page provides a biographical and theological summary of Saint John the Baptist, detailing his miraculous birth, his role as the prophesied herald of Christ, his ascetic lifestyle, and his martyrdom under Herod Antipas.</summary>
<keywords>John the Baptist, Zacharias, Elizabeth, Prophecy, Isaiah, Malachi, Elijah, Herod Antipas, Herodias, Martyrdom, Liturgical Calendar</keywords>

This column presents a reproduction of the Old Babylonian cuneiform <note>the wedge-shaped writing system used in ancient Mesopotamia</note> script from the Stele <note>an upright stone monument</note> of Hammurabi, specifically Column 40. The text spans approximately 21 rows, beginning from line 8 and extending through line 28. The wedges are sharp and clearly defined, representing the formal monumental style of the 18th century BCE. In this section of the epilogue, Hammurabi traditionally emphasizes his role as a "shepherd" to his people and his commitment to justice.

<column-break/>

<margin>30</margin>
<margin>35</margin>
<margin>40</margin>
<margin>45</margin>
The second column continues the transcription of the cuneiform text, containing approximately 20 rows of script representing lines 29 through 48. The characters are densely packed within the vertical registers, maintaining the consistent and authoritative style of a royal legal proclamation. This portion of the text typically contains the King's instructions for future rulers to respect the laws he has established.

**Key Terminology**
*   **Hammurabi:** The sixth king of the First Babylonian Dynasty, famous for his legal code.
*   **Code of Hammurabi:** A foundational legal text of the ancient world.
*   **Akkadian:** The Semitic language used in ancient Mesopotamia; the language in which these laws are written.
*   **Cuneiform:** Writing made by pressing a stylus into clay or carving into stone to create wedge-shaped marks.
*   **Old Babylonian:** The specific dialect and historical period of the Babylonian Empire during Hammurabi's reign.
*   **Stele:** The large, finger-shaped black stone (diorite) on which the code was originally carved.
*   **Law Code:** A formal, systematic collection of laws.

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI PLATE 73
->73<-

<margin>Col. XL.</margin>
<margin>50</margin>
In my protective shadow, I have spread peace over the city; I have held the people of the lands of Sumer and Akkad <note>the southern and northern regions of ancient Mesopotamia</note> safely in my lap. Through my **protective spirit**, they have prospered. I have governed them in peace; by my wisdom, I have sheltered them.

<margin>55</margin>
So that the strong might not oppress the weak, and to provide justice to the orphan and the widow, I have inscribed my precious words upon my monument in Babylon <note>the capital city of Hammurabi's empire</note>, the city whose head the gods Anu and Enlil <note>the highest deities in the Mesopotamian pantheon</note> have raised high, and within **Esagila**, the temple whose foundations are as firm as heaven and earth.

<margin>60</margin>
I have set up this stone to pronounce the law of the land, to settle disputes, and to render justice to the oppressed. I am the **King of Justice**, to whom the sun-god Shamash <note>the divine judge and god of justice</note> has entrusted the law.

<margin>65</margin>
My words are weighty; my deeds have no equal. Only to the fool are they empty; to the wise, they are a source of eternal wonder.

<column-break/>

<margin>70</margin>
Let any man who is oppressed and has a legal case come before my statue as the **King of Justice** <note>original: *šar mīšarim*</note>. Let him have my inscribed stele <note>upright stone monument</note> read aloud to him. Let him hear my precious words, and let my monument clarify his case for him.

<margin>75</margin>

# EPISTLE
<sig>Q 4</sig>

<margin>See Basil, Letter 192.</margin>
...which not only has no one done before, but it seems that no mention has been made of it from then until this day, except in this edition, in which it first appears. However, to speak frankly, it does not entirely satisfy me, and I suspect that in some places it is defective <note>original: *mancam*; meaning crippled or incomplete</note> (since it was found in only one manuscript). Nevertheless, because a certain trust is better than an uncertain expectation, we wished to make it a matter of public record <note>original: *publici iuris facere*; a legal term for publishing</note> just as it is, so that everyone might know that we have omitted nothing of those things which pertain to this matter. For this reason, we ask you again and again to look kindly upon our work; and if anything occurs to you that seems incorrectly placed or overlooked in this edition, please signify this to us out of your kindness. For in this way, you will make us more eager to attempt similar projects, and you yourselves will make greater progress in fine literature. Farewell.

->Dated from our library <note>original: *Musæo*; literally "place of the Muses," used by Renaissance scholars to mean a study or library</note> on the day before the Ides of January,<-
->In the year 1573 since the birth of Christ.<- <note>January 12, 1573</note>

---

But if any of you should wish to compare this edition of ours with others, he will easily understand how much has been achieved by us. For in many places, we have not only restored the reading of the text, but we have also explained the meanings themselves. <margin>A Greek proverb.</margin> And here there comes to my mind that Greek proverb: "Often even a gardener has spoken a very timely word." <note>original: Πολλάκι καὶ κηπωρὸς ἀνὴρ μάλα καίριον εἶπεν</note> Which we have rendered into Latin thus: *Often even a cabbage has spoken opportunely.* <note>The translator plays on the Greek word for gardener (*keporos*) by using the Latin word for a garden vegetable (*holus*) to humorously suggest that even a simple or "green" edition can be useful.</note> For in this way, even this edition of ours, although it may not be perfect in every detail <note>original: *omnibus numeris absoluta*; a Latin idiom for "perfect in all its parts"</note>, nevertheless seems likely to be not unfruitful. As for the rest, we pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that He may bless you and your studies. Again, farewell.

<page-num>403</page-num>
<header>On the Grace of Christ.</header>

# ARTICLE VI.
## Is it possible, through the grace of Christ, for a person in this state of fallen nature to remain without any venial sin for an entire day, or even a lifetime?

<margin>Proposition 1.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 63.</margin>
I respond firstly: Although a person in the state of fallen nature <note>original: *naturae lapsae*; the theological state of humanity after the "Fall of Man," characterized by a weakened will and inclination toward sin</note> can avoid individual venial sins <note>minor or "pardonable" sins that do not fully rupture a person's relationship with God, as opposed to "mortal" sins</note>, they cannot avoid all of them collectively. That is, they cannot avoid committing any venial sin whatsoever throughout their entire life without a special privilege from God, such as that held by the Blessed Virgin Mary. This proposition is directed against the Pelagians <note>a group following the monk Pelagius, who argued that humans could achieve moral perfection through their own will without divine grace</note>, and it is a matter of faith according to the Council of Trent, Session 6, Canon 23. It is derived from St. Augustine, who frequently teaches that while there have been some Just people who lived "without crime"—meaning without mortal sin—no one has lived without venial sin.

<margin>Proposition 2.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapters 1 and 5.</margin>
I respond secondly: Speaking in absolute terms, it is possible for a human, through the grace of God, to abstain from every sin—even venial sin—for their entire life or for a long period of time. This is the common position held against Luther and Calvin, who argued that a person sins, at least slightly, in every deed they perform. This is proven by the words of St. Augustine: *We do not deny that such a person can exist, to whom a good will is given to such an extent that they have no sin at all; however, we say this has not happened except in the Blessed Virgin.*

The reasoning is as follows: there is no inherent necessity to sin, and the grace of Christ is sufficient for avoiding any sin, even the slightest. Therefore, through that grace, a person is able to abstain from all sin. You might ask: if there is no necessity to sin, why is it said that all venial sins cannot be avoided? I respond that this does not arise from an absolute impossibility, but from a lack of vigilance and from human frailty. The human mind cannot always be so intensely focused that it prevents some disordered impulse from creeping in <note>original: *subrepat*; suggests an unintentional or stealthy occurrence</note>, or some less-than-deliberate action from occurring, which constitutes a venial sin.

<meta>catchword: That</meta>

<summary>This page discusses whether it is possible for a human to live without committing any minor (venial) sins. It concludes that while it is theoretically possible through God's grace, in practice, human frailty and a lack of constant vigilance make it impossible to avoid all such sins throughout a lifetime without a special divine privilege.</summary>
<keywords>Grace of Christ, venial sin, fallen nature, Pelagians, Council of Trent, Virgin Mary, St. Augustine, Martin Luther, John Calvin, human frailty</keywords>

-># ON THE SACRAMENT OF PENANCE.<-

<margin>Question 159.</margin>
...ment and encouragement, which should therefore be moderate and not too long, so that other penitents are not overly burdened by the delay and become weary.

Secondly, the confessor should not inquire into the names of accomplices, unless it is strictly required to understand the type or gravity of the sin; for example, if the penitent says they have sinned with a relative, the priest must inquire what degree of kinship they share. See <term>St. Thomas</term> <note>original: "S. Thom." — referring to St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences*, Book 4, Distinction 19, Question 2, Article 2, Response to the 4th point.

### QUESTION 160.

*Can a confessor give a penitent permission to sin?*

Response: No; and this for three reasons.

<margin>Summa Silvestrina, entry 'Confessor' 1, § 10.</margin>
First, because a confessor does not have the power to grant a dispensation <note>an exemption from a law</note> from divine law, which prohibits all sin.

Second, because no one can give another permission to sin, as this would be giving permission to offend God—which is against the love of God—and because no one can give another permission to do what they themselves cannot do. A confessor cannot sin himself; therefore, he cannot give another person permission to sin.

If, however, a penitent were to say to the confessor: "Father, I am in such a state of need that it is necessary for me to steal or to lie," could the confessor then say to him: "Very well, steal," or "Lie"?

Response: He can in no way say this to him; because (as was stated) he cannot give permission to sin;

<column-break/>

and also because, by natural law, everyone is bound to prefer to die rather than offend God through a mortal sin <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal" sin is a grave action that leads to a total break with God's grace</note>.

Third and finally, because that would be to approve of the sin and be a participant in it, which is against right reason and against the law of God.

If the penitent says that he cannot otherwise escape death except by lying or stealing, the confessor must respond that he ought rather to choose death than mortal sin.

Note, however, two things here:

First, that although a confessor cannot give permission to sin, he can nevertheless advise the penitent to choose the lesser of two evils of punishment <note>Original: "malis poenae" — referring to physical hardships or worldly consequences rather than moral faults</note> in order to avoid the greater.

<margin>St. Thomas, Summa Theologica, Part 2-2, Question 62, Article 7; and others commonly.</margin>
Second, if the penitent is in such extreme necessity that, according to right reason, he may take another's property to sustain his life, then the confessor can tell him that in such a case, taking another's property is not theft. Instead, it is the use of his own right, because in a case of extreme necessity, all things are common <note>This refers to the medieval legal principle that in a life-or-death situation, the right to survive outweighs private property laws</note>.

### QUESTION 161.

*Can a confessor reveal a confession?*

Response: No; and he is bound to this under the penalty of mortal sin and other very grave penalties of both divine and canon law <note>Church law</note>.

<margin>Lateran Council under Innocent III, Canon 21.</margin>
First, by divine law: because the "seal of confession" was instituted by Christ the Lord, so that penitents might securely confess their sins without fear of them being revealed.

Second, by canon law: as is clear in the chapter *Everyone of both sexes* <note>original: "Omnis utriusque sexus" — the famous decree of the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 requiring yearly confession</note>, regarding penance and remission, where it is said: *Let him take great care, however, that he does not in any way betray the sinner by word, sign, or any other means.*

Cc 4
<meta>catchword: and also</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the moral and legal boundaries of a priest acting as a confessor, specifically forbidding the granting of permission to sin and upholding the absolute secrecy of the "seal of confession." It includes a notable legal exception regarding "extreme necessity," where taking food or property to stay alive is not considered theft.</summary>

In the context of the basalt stela, an erasure occurs where the ancient craftsman physically ground down the stone surface to remove a mistake before carving the correct <term>cuneiform</term><note>A system of writing used in ancient Mesopotamia, characterized by wedge-shaped marks made with a reed stylus.</note> signs over the top. This plate is essential for epigraphers to understand the physical history of the monument's creation.</meta>

# THE CODE OF HAMMURABI: PLATE 103 <note>CIII is the Roman numeral for 103.</note>

->**A Map of the Ancient Near East**<-

This map illustrates the vast geographical landscape of the world known to the ancient Babylonians and the archaeological sites where the legacy of King Hammurabi was rediscovered. It stretches from the Mediterranean Sea in the west to the Persian highlands in the east.

### Geographical Locations and Landmarks

**Europe and the Northern Seas**
Europe, Constantinople, Bosphorus, Dardanelles, and the Black Sea.

**Asia Minor and Armenia**
Asia Minor, Smyrna, the Halys <note>A major river in central Anatolia, now known as the Kızılırmak.</note>, the Taurus Mountains, Armenia, Lake Van, and Lake Urumiah.

**Syria and the Mediterranean Coast**
Cyprus, the Mediterranean Sea, Iskanderun, Aleppo, Karkar, Palmyra, the Syrian Desert, Damascus, Palestine, and Jerusalem.

**Egypt**
Alexandria, Port Said, Lower Egypt, and Cairo.

**Mesopotamia and Babylonia**
The Euphrates <note>River</note> and the Tigris <note>River</note>, along with their tributaries: the Balikh <note>River</note>, the Khabur <note>River</note>, the Upper Zab <note>River</note>, and the Lower Zab <note>River</note>. 
Cities and archaeological sites include: Mosul, Nineveh, Assur (Kala'at Sherkat), the Diyala <note>River</note>, Dur-Ilu, Baghdad, Agade, Shatt-el-Nil, Sippar (Abu Habba), Cutha (Tel Ibrahim), Babylon (Hillah), Kish (El Oheimer), Borsippa (Birs Nimrud), Nippur (Nuffar), Shuruppak (Fara), Diwanieh, Erech (Warka), Larsa (Senkereh), Lagash (Tello), Shirpurla, Ur (Mugheir), and Eridu (Abu Shahrein).

**Persia and the East**
Persia, the Caspian Sea, Ecbatana (Hamadan), Susa, the Kerkha <note>River</note>, the Karun <note>River</note>, Basra, and the Persian Gulf.

**Southern Regions**
Arabia

### Key Terms

<term>Hammurabi</term>: The sixth king of the First Babylonian Dynasty (reigned c. 1792–1750 BCE), who enacted one of the earliest and most complete written legal codes.
<term>Mesopotamia</term>: Meaning "between two rivers" in Greek, this region lies between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
<term>Babylonia</term>: An ancient cultural region in central-southern Mesopotamia, with the city of Babylon as its capital.
<term>Sumer</term>: The southernmost region of ancient Mesopotamia, home to the world's earliest civilization.
<term>Asia Minor</term>: The westernmost protrusion of Asia, making up the majority of modern-day Turkey.
<term>Nineveh</term>: An ancient Assyrian city of Upper Mesopotamia, located on the outskirts of modern Mosul.
<term>Susa</term>: An ancient city in the lower Zagros Mountains where the stela containing the Code of Hammurabi was discovered in 1901.
<term>Ur</term>: An important Sumerian city-state located at the site of modern Tell el-Muqayyar.
<term>Assyria</term>: A major Mesopotamian kingdom and empire of the ancient Near East.
<term>Akkad</term>: The seat of the Akkadian Empire, the first ancient empire of Mesopotamia.

<summary>This page presents a detailed geographical index and map of the Ancient Near East, identifying the major cities, rivers, and regions relevant to the study of the Code of Hammurabi and Mesopotamian history.</summary>
<keywords>Hammurabi, Mesopotamia, Babylonia, Euphrates, Tigris, Sumer, Asia Minor, Nineveh, Susa, Ur, Assyria, Akkad, Geography</keywords>

# The Life of Sir Thomas More

<term>Sir Thomas More <note>Sir Thomas More (1478–1535) was a legendary English lawyer, philosopher, and Lord Chancellor to King Henry VIII. He is most famous for his book "Utopia" and for his eventual execution after refusing to recognize the King as the head of the Church of England.</note></term>
